message.content:
You are a research agent for a BMW hackathon app (AI that derives prioritized *customer-facing* requirements for successor BMW vehicles: 1 Series F70, 5 Series G60 / China LWB G68, 7 Series G70; markets EU, US, CN, plus RoW = Japan/Korea; successor launches ~2028–2031).

Work ONLY in this directory: /Users/atahankilic/Documents/ehl-munich-final/.claude/worktrees/v2 . Read `foundation/documents/plan-v2.md` (pillar P2) and skim `foundation/documents/competitor-landscape.md` and `foundation/documents/knowledge-base.md` (trust tiers T1–T3) for conventions. Do NOT edit code, the DB, or any existing file. Do NOT read anything in `challange information document/` (confidential, not needed). Do not send any BMW-internal data to web searches.

TASK — "Regulatory & compliance radar". BMW's brief says regulatory/homologation requirements are OUT of scope as outputs, so we use regulation as context, trigger and gate: which binding or upcoming regulations (and quasi-regulatory rating programs like Euro NCAP, C-NCAP, IIHS) change what customers experience in the car, per market, between 2025 and ~2032. Use WebSearch/WebFetch. Prefer T1 sources (official regulator/legal text: EUR-Lex, UNECE, MIIT/SAMR/CAC, NHTSA/Federal Register, Euro NCAP protocols), then T2 (Reuters, Automotive News, law-firm briefings). Verify every claim; record URL, publisher, publish date, retrieved date 2026-10-11, and a short exact quote.

Candidates to verify (and find others): Euro NCAP 2026 protocol rewarding physical controls (indicators, hazards, horn, wipers, eCall); China MIIT mandatory standard on door handles (mechanical release, flush handles) from 2027; China MIIT rules after the 2025 Xiaomi SU7 crash on L2 ADAS marketing terms ("autonomous", "smart driving"), OTA updates needing approval, beta testing ban; China L2 ADAS mandatory national standard; China data security / car data export rules (CAC); EU GSR2 (ISA speed limit warning, driver drowsiness/attention, DDAW/ADDW, EDR) and customer annoyance with ISA beeps; UN R155/R156 cybersecurity/software updates (consequence: OTA, feature unavailability e.g. in older cars); UN R157/R171 (DCAS) hands-off driving in EU; EU Data Act (Sept 2025) customer access to vehicle data; EU battery regulation (battery passport, state of health); Euro 7 (brake dust, battery durability — customer-facing consequence: battery health guarantee); EU AFIR (charging payment by card, price transparency); EU CO2 fleet targets 2025–2035 and the 2035 combustion phase-out debate (consequence: powertrain availability per market); US: NHTSA AEB rule FMVSS 127 (2029), US EV tax credit end (Sept 2025), US tariffs; US ban on Chinese connected-vehicle software/hardware (BIS rule, MY2027/2030) — consequence for infotainment partners; China NEV purchase tax changes 2026–2027; China mandatory requirements on screen/HMI distraction if any; EU right-to-repair; accessibility; seat/child-seat ISOFIX/i-Size; Japan/Korea where relevant. Also mirror-cameras, light signatures (illuminated grilles regulations), sound (AVAS), subscription/feature-on-demand consumer-protection rulings.

For each regulation produce: id (REG-XX-nn), jurisdiction (EU/US/CN/UNECE/JP/KR/global), title, instrument type (law / mandatory standard / rating program / guidance), status (in force / adopted / proposed / debated), key dates (adopted, applies to new types, applies to all new registrations), affected categories from this list [Exterior, Interior, Comfort & Space, Infotainment & Digital, Driving Experience, Powertrain (as experienced), Range & Charging, Driver Assistance (as experienced), Variants & Packages, Design & Quality Perception], customer-facing consequence (one plain sentence: what changes for the driver), opportunity (how a customer-facing requirement can turn this into value), risk/conflict (which kind of feature would conflict — e.g. hidden flush door handles, touch-only hazard switch, "autopilot" naming), affected models (F70/G60/G68/G70 + markets), trust tier, sources [{url, publisher, published, retrieved, quote}].

OUTPUTS (exactly these two files):
1. `data/seed/regulations.json` — a JSON array of the objects above (valid JSON; keys snake_case).
2. `foundation/documents/regulatory-radar.md` — concise human doc: purpose + scope line (regulation as context/trigger/gate, never an output spec — BMW brief), a table per market, then "Top 8 customer-facing implications for successor BMWs" with citations, then "Unverified / conflicting" section. Plain, clear English, short sentences.

Quality bar: only include items you verified from a source you actually opened; mark uncertain items status "unverified" rather than inventing. Aim for 20–35 regulations. Final message to me: counts per jurisdiction, the 8 implications in one line each, and anything surprising.

# CLAUDE.md

@AGENTS.md

## Claude-specific notes

- `AGENTS.md` (imported above) is the canonical rule set shared with Codex and other agents — edit rules there, not here, so both stay in sync.
- The project memory is `foundation/` — read `foundation/README.md` for the read/write protocol. Prefer it over personal memory for anything project-related.
- The app's LLM provider is **OpenAI** (D-006) — don't add the Anthropic SDK or Claude model IDs to the app code.

# AGENTS.md

Hackathon project for the **BMW "AI for Product Decision Making"** challenge: an AI app that turns customer feedback, BMW product/sales data and web research into **prioritized, evidence-linked customer requirements** for successor BMW vehicles, with a **product manager (PM) in the loop** and a **full audit trail**.

**Portfolio-level by design:** multiple models, markets, shared platforms (CLAR, FAAR → Neue Klasse) and plants from day one. The 5 Series (G60 + China LWB G68) is the deepest example; F70 and G70 use the same pipeline. **LLM provider: OpenAI.** Stack: Python 3.12/uv, LangGraph, SQLite + sqlite-vec, no graph DB, Streamlit (D-015–D-020).

## Session start — mandatory

Read, in order (short):
1. `foundation/STATE.md` — phase, team, demo path, next steps, budget
2. `foundation/OPEN_QUESTIONS.md` — the "Open" section; check for blockers
3. `foundation/DECISIONS.md` — the **Index** table at the top; open full entries only when relevant. Don't re-open settled decisions without new info.

Then read only what your task needs:

| If your task touches… | Read |
|---|---|
| Scope, deliverables, what BMW asked | `documents/challenge-brief.md` |
| BMW data files, counts, quirks | `documents/data-inventory.md` |
| Stack / tooling, budget guard | `documents/tech-stack.md` |
| Workflow, entities, audit rules | `documents/architecture.md` |
| Requirement fields, evidence levels, scoring | `documents/requirement-model.md` |
| Research agents, trust tiers, brand/feasibility checks | `documents/knowledge-base.md` |
| Platforms, plants, BMW sales (cited) | `documents/portfolio-reference.md` (long — search it) |
| Competitors, trends, brand guardrails (cited) | `documents/competitor-landscape.md` (long — search it) |
| BMW Group Report 2025: deliveries, EV share, R&D, NK, digital | `documents/bmw-annual-report-2025.md` |
| Unknown term or code | `documents/glossary.md` |
| Fresh clone / setup | `foundation/README.md` → Fresh clone |

## Session end — mandatory

- Update `foundation/STATE.md` (phase, in progress, next up, one-line session log entry with date).
- Log every decision as `D-xxx` in `foundation/DECISIONS.md`; new questions as `Q-xxx` in `foundation/OPEN_QUESTIONS.md`.
- If code changes the stack, schema, or workflow, update the matching doc in `foundation/documents/` in the same change.

## Core rules

1. **Raw data is read-only and confidential.** `challange information document/` (typo is the real folder name) is git-ignored — never modify, move or commit it; never send it anywhere except the agreed LLM provider. Derived data goes to git-ignored `data/`.
2. **Stay in scope.** Customer-facing requirements only (features, equipment, comfort, space, usability, infotainment/digital, design & quality perception, driving experience, range/charging as experienced, variants/packages). **Out:** regulatory/homologation, engineering/component specs, pricing/business cases (rough effort as a factor is OK).
3. **Traceability is non-negotiable.** Every finding links to ≥1 source item; every requirement links to ≥1 finding. Keep provenance (file, sheet, row/ID, URL + date for web).
4. **Evidence vs. assumption.** Always separate evidence-backed statements from forward-looking assumptions (3–5 yr horizon); surface conflicting evidence instead of hiding it.
5. **The PM decides, never the AI.** AI only creates/edits in `proposed` status; `approved`/`rejected`/`deferred` require a human actor + rationale. Exception (D-013): AI may recompute *scores* of any requirement (logged); priority/status changes stay proposals.
6. **Audit everything, append-only.** Every change to requirement content, score, priority, evidence or status → an `audit_event` (actor human/ai/system, timestamp, before/after, rationale, model for AI).
7. **Portfolio, not one-offs.** Brands, models, markets, platforms and plants are data/config — never hardcode a derivative or market. Requirements can target several derivative × market combinations.
8. **Brand & segment fit.** Every requirement must fit the brand and the segment (no "cheap efficiency hatch" from BMW, no budget Rolls-Royce). Brand-fit `fail` blocks approval unless a PM overrides with rationale.
9. **Plant & platform feasibility.** A recommendation must be buildable: the derivative's platform and a plant that builds it can serve that market in time (incl. Neue Klasse transition). Used as a feasibility filter only — never output engineering specs. Whether a `fail` blocks approval is open (Q-010: BMW lists "architecture" as out of scope).
10. **Web evidence is cited evidence.** Competitor, sales, demand and expectation facts come from web research with URL, publish/retrieve date and trust tier (T1–T3). LLM opinions are never stored as sources; unverified user claims stay flagged until verified.
11. **Explainable prioritization.** Every score has a visible factor breakdown and plain-language rationale.
12. **OpenAI for all LLM work**; model names via env (`OPENAI_MODEL_*`). Secrets live in `.env` (git-ignored); commit `.env.example` only.
13. **Markets are different customers.** Climate, usage and culture differ — segment findings by market and score/prioritize each derivative × market separately; surface cross-market conflicts (D-011).
14. **Future, not just past.** Derive what customers will need at successor launch (3–5 yr) from predecessor feedback + competitors + trends; tag horizon, Kano class and assumptions (D-012).
15. **Living process, not a one-shot list.** ~2-year process: every prioritization run is snapshotted; AI only *proposes* priority/status changes with their cause; PM decides; history is always visible (D-013).
16. **$100 OpenAI budget, total.** Cheap model (`gpt-6-luna`) for bulk extraction/classification/summaries; `gpt-6.1-sol` only for reasoning-heavy steps; all calls through the budget-guarded wrapper; Flex/Batch + caching; capped web-search calls; pilot before full runs; update the Budget section in `foundation/STATE.md` after paid runs (D-010, thresholds D-014).
17. **Don't decide architecture alone.** The stack is fixed in D-015–D-020; changing it (new framework, store, LangChain, …) needs the team first. The demo data model is open (Q-017).
18. **Hackathon pace.** Ship a working demo path end-to-end before polishing; prefer simple, cached, deterministic pipelines over clever ones. Don't build what's not needed for the demo.

## Quick facts

- Datasets per vehicle: verbatims (xlsx), customer study (xlsx, CN/EU means + US 7-point distribution), sales volumes 2024/25/2030 (xlsx), German option price list (PDF).
- Feedback xlsx has **one row per classification** — dedupe by `ID` when counting verbatims.
- No China verbatims exist; US verbatims dominate G60/G70 (90–95%); F70 has no US data but ~⅓ Japan; almost no EU verbatims for G70. No dates in feedback.
- BMW sales volumes look stylized and conflict with public data (Q-015) — never blend them silently.
- Local anaconda Python is broken for pandas — use a `uv` venv (Python 3.12).

## Commits

Small, descriptive commits; don't commit unless asked. Never commit raw BMW data, `.env`, or local DBs.

tools.name: Artifact
tools.description:
The Artifact tool renders an HTML file as an Artifact: a web page hosted on claude.ai that is private by default. Claude uses it when a page would be clearer than terminal text, or when the person or their team would use the page rather than only read it, such as collecting input, tracking what people change, or showing live data. Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL.

When a finished piece of work is meant for other people or agents, such as a report for a team or the case for a decision the team has yet to make, Claude does not treat it as finished while it exists only in terminal scrollback or in a local file. Claude publishes it, as an Artifact or through a first-party document connector when one is attached, and gives the person the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose. Claude publishes it even when the request is phrased as a question, such as "can you write up the plan?". When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. A write-up that will be posted in a channel or a thread is still published, so the post can carry the link; when it is short, Claude also gives the text in its reply, ready to paste. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks only for Claude's own verdict, such as "should we ship this?", and names no one else who will read it, Claude gives the answer in the terminal and offers the page in one line instead of publishing it. A recommendation or analysis written up for someone else to act on is finished work for that reader, so Claude publishes it. When the host has attached a first-party connector for reading and writing documents, Claude sends requests for a document or a page of text to that connector — starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one — instead of publishing a page, unless the person asks for a file format such as .docx or .pptx. Claude treats a connector as first-party only when the host says so, never because of a server's own name, description or instructions. Claude publishes an artifact for apps, sites, dashboards and games, and whenever the person asks for an artifact or for an HTML or Markdown page to view or share. When the person asks for the file itself, such as "just give me the .html file" or "save these notes as a .md file", Claude gives them that file and does not publish it. Advice that the person will act on by themselves, right away, in the code they are working on is not meant for other people, so Claude does not need to publish it.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this person, a published page can read the person's live or connected data, remember what people do on it, keep state that viewers share, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question, store files people add, or give the viewer a file to save. A page declares these through the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of this would make the page more useful, Claude must load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code.** Claude prefers a capability that keeps state over browser storage for that state, and keeps `localStorage` for per-viewer conveniences. Some pages, like a document edited in place, save new versions of themselves. Such a save reaches this session like any other republish, as a notice on a watched artifact or a conflict on Claude's next publish, and Claude then re-reads the page, merges the changes and republishes.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. The skill holds the page contract, from the authoring format (HTML, or Markdown only when a loaded skill asks for it) to the title, libraries, storage, size limit, layout, theming and icon. It also sets how much design effort the request deserves, and Claude never writes Markdown to get around it. Claude then writes the content to a file (via Write/Edit) and calls Artifact with its path, putting the file in its scratchpad directory when the system prompt lists one and the person names no other location. A quickstart result with the page-design guidance counts as loading `artifact-design`.

**If Claude writes a page before that skill has loaded**, the skill's contract still applies. Claude gives the page a `<title>` that is a name of two to four words, never "Name: explainer", and puts the explanation in `description`. Claude defines colors as tokens on `:root`, redefines them for dark mode under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded by `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, and gives `body` an explicit background. Claude loads external scripts only from cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, unpkg.com, cdn.tailwindcss.com or code.jquery.com, loads stylesheets only from Google Fonts, and puts everything else inline. Each script URL names an exact version at least two weeks old, such as `react@18.3.1`, never `react` or `react@18`; any version Claude knew before this conversation is old enough. Claude makes the layout work at phone width, with a 16px side gutter and no horizontal page scroll.

**Format**: Claude always authors the page as `.html`, and publishes a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly asks for one. When the person shares a Markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, Claude builds an HTML page from its content, keeping its substance and designing the page as it would any other artifact rather than transcribing the Markdown one to one.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage`, `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB work, but each artifact has its own origin and what a page stores lives only in that viewer's browser. It survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices or Claude. It can come back empty, or the accessor can throw, in a private window, with cleared or blocked site data, in previews or during thumbnail capture, so Claude wraps every read and write in try/catch and makes the page render correctly without it. Claude uses it only for per-viewer conveniences, such as a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section or an unsent draft, and never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers or be read back by Claude. That state belongs in a runtime capability.

**Size**: Claude keeps the rendered page at 16MB or smaller, and embedded `data:` URIs count toward that limit.

**Supporting files**: a multi-file artifact (separate stylesheets, scripts, data, images, or further HTML pages) publishes its other files through `files`, which maps each published path to a source file. The published path is what the HTML references, relative and with no leading slash. Only the page itself is wrapped in a document skeleton at publish time: an HTML file in `files` is another page served without one, so Claude starts each with its own `<!doctype html>`, charset and viewport metas and base styles, or, without the doctype, it renders in quirks mode with browser defaults. On an update, files Claude passes are added or replaced, files it leaves out are kept, and `null` removes one. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks only for Claude's own verdict, such as "should we ship this?", and names no one else who will read it, Claude gives the answer in the terminal and offers the page in one line instead of publishing it. A recommendation or analysis written up for someone else to act on is finished work for that reader, so Claude publishes it. **Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

schema.name: Edit
schema.description:

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.description:
Deliver your final report to the agent that spawned you (your caller). Use it once, for that hand-off only: when your work is complete, call SubagentHandback({message: <your full report>}). The call ends your run, so do everything else first and put everything your caller needs in that one report. It is not a messaging channel: do not use it for progress updates or questions.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Euro NCAP's 2026 protocol would reward physical controls for five functions: indicators, hazard lights, the horn, windscreen wipers, and the eCall SOS function. These are news reports, not the official protocol, so I couldn't verify the exact wording.

- **Scope:** Euro NCAP wants separate physical controls for basic functions, not a full return to buttons. Euro NCAP is not insisting on everything being its own button or switch.
- **Scoring:** These functions must be accessible via physical buttons, stalks, or dials to achieve a maximum score in the vehicle's safety rating. However, they will only count for 5 out of the 100 points in the 'Safe Driving' category.
- **Timing:** Reports say the rules take effect in January 2026. One source describes the new criteria as "New assessments of the human-machine interface (HMI) are introduced" in its 2026 criteria, and says they focus on "evaluating the placement, clarity, and ease of use of essential controls".
- **Enforcement:** Euro NCAP is not a government regulator, so it has no power to mandate carmakers use physical controls for those functions.
- **eCall:** The eCall function is mandatory in the European Union for several years, and it automatically dials the local emergency number in the event of a serious car accident.
- **Affected cars:** Tesla is cited as the most exposed, since it recently ditched physical stalks that instead move the turn signal functions to haptic buttons on the steering wheel.

The MIIT rule is a mandatory national standard, GB 48001-2026, "Safety Technical Requirements for Automotive Door Handles," and it takes effect January 1, 2027. The main points:

- **Scope:** Regulators are targeting concealed, electronically operated handles. One report says the standard applies to M1 and N1 vehicles and multi-purpose cargo trucks, with other vehicle types expected to reference it. The standard explicitly applies to M1 and N1 category vehicles and multi-purpose cargo trucks, while other vehicle types are expected to reference it for compliance.
- **Mechanical release:** Each door, except the tailgate, needs an exterior handle with a mechanical release. Interior handles also need a mechanical backup, even on vehicles with electric handles. Under the standard, every vehicle door other than the tailgate must have a mechanical exterior handle. Interior handles must also have a mechanical backup release, even when the vehicle uses electric door handles. (That second item comes from the draft stage, so the final wording may differ.)
- **Performance:** Vehicles with electric release latches must let doors open via the mechanical release handle without tools after testing. Exterior handles also need a minimum hand operation space of 60 mm × 20 mm × 25 mm.
- **Timeline (sources conflict):** One outlet reports that newly approved models must fully comply by Jan 1, 2028, and models already approved must meet all requirements by Jan 1, 2029. Another says newly submitted vehicle models must comply with most requirements starting in 2027, and all vehicles sold in the market must fully meet the standard by 2029. The exact compliance dates for new models are therefore unclear from these results.
- **Open questions:** One analysis notes that specific details on how these requirements will be implemented in practice, particularly the exact technical standards for mechanical overrides, have yet to be fully clarified.

Tesla has said it is redesigning its handles, but it is unclear when those changes will make their way into production.

China's first mandatory national standard for L2 combined driver assistance is GB 47955-2026, and it takes effect on January 1, 2027.

- **Issuer and status:** The MIIT organized the standard, which received approval from the State Administration for Market Regulation and the Standardization Administration. The ministry announced its release in early July 2026, and the standard was recently approved and released by those two agencies.
- **Scope:** It sets safety requirements for basic single-lane systems, basic multi-lane systems, and navigation-assisted driving systems. It also covers functions, data recording, manufacturer safety guarantees, human-machine interaction, user instructions, and user training.
- **Tiers:** Per Gasgoo, basic single-lane systems support adaptive cruise and lane keeping but block automatic lane changes, multi-lane systems allow lane changes only when the driver's turn signal triggers them, and NOA permits automatic lane changes and ramp navigation but strictly forbids crossing solid lines.
- **Driver responsibility:** An earlier draft explicitly states that during operation the driver must remain the primary agent responsible for dynamic driving tasks.
- **Market enforcement:** One report says the standard makes driver monitoring, obstacle detection at 120m@80km/h, and lockouts for misuse compulsory market entry rules. Treat that detail with some caution, since I only saw it in this one source.
- **Motivation:** MIIT data cited in the coverage says penetration of new passenger cars with combined driver assistance reached 70 percent since the beginning of 2026, while NOA-equipped models exceeded 30 percent.
- **Timeline:** The draft was opened for comment in April 2026, with public comments solicited from April 16 to 22, 2026.

The search did not turn up anything on a 2027 deadline beyond the effective date, so the "2027" in your query most likely refers to this January 1, 2027 implementation date.

China's first mandatory national standard for L2 combined driver assistance is GB 47955-2026, and it takes effect on January 1, 2027.

- **Issuer and status:** The MIIT organized the standard, which received approval from the State Administration for Market Regulation and the Standardization Administration. The ministry announced its release in early July 2026, and the standard was recently approved and released by those two agencies.
- **Scope:** It sets safety requirements for basic single-lane systems, basic multi-lane systems, and navigation-assisted driving systems. It also covers functions, data recording, manufacturer safety guarantees, human-machine interaction, user instructions, and user training.
- **Tiers:** Per Gasgoo, basic single-lane systems support adaptive cruise and lane keeping but block automatic lane changes, multi-lane systems allow lane changes only when the driver's turn signal triggers them, and NOA permits automatic lane changes and ramp navigation but strictly forbids crossing solid lines.
- **Driver responsibility:** An earlier draft explicitly states that during operation the driver must remain the primary agent responsible for dynamic driving tasks.
- **Market enforcement:** One report says the standard makes driver monitoring, obstacle detection at 120m@80km/h, and lockouts for misuse compulsory market entry rules. Treat that detail with some caution, since I only saw it in this one source.
- **Motivation:** MIIT data cited in the coverage says penetration of new passenger cars with combined driver assistance reached 70 percent since the beginning of 2026, while NOA-equipped models exceeded 30 percent.
- **Timeline:** The draft was opened for comment in April 2026, with public comments solicited from April 16 to 22, 2026.

The search did not turn up anything on a 2027 deadline beyond the effective date, so the "2027" in your query most likely refers to this January 1, 2027 implementation date.

Euro NCAP's 2026 protocols add a new human-machine interface (HMI) assessment under the Safe Driving stage, and physical controls are a central part of it.

- **Structure:** The update features an overhaul of vehicle testing and scoring, with a new methodology built around four stages: Safe Driving, Crash Avoidance, Crash Protection, and Post-Crash Safety.
- **HMI assessment:** The Stage One assessment looks at how essential controls are placed, how clear they are, and how easy they are to use. It also checks whether physical buttons exist for commonly used functions, which consumer feedback suggests can reduce distraction.
- **Scoring weight:** In the Driver Engagement protocol (v1.1, October 2025), General Vehicle Controls carries 5 of 30 driver-engagement points, and its acceptance criteria aim to promote HMI designs that minimize driver distraction (gaze off-road duration).
- **Test procedure:** The SD 203 procedure grades how each function is implemented, from direct physical input (buttons, pedals, switches) through direct voice and touch input to menu-based touch input, with menu depth being a factor. Its implementation date is 1st January 2026.
- **Rating validity:** Euro NCAP says a car's safety rating is valid for up to six years from the date it is awarded.

The search returned Euro NCAP's own pages and protocol PDFs, so these details come from the primary source. I did not check whether any specific 2026 model has been rated under the new HMI criteria.

The main document is the joint MIIT and SAMR Notice No. 45 [2025] on admission, recall, and OTA software upgrades for intelligent connected vehicles. The search returned nothing dated 2026, so I can't confirm whether it has been amended since.

- **Issuance and timing:** Law firm CMS says the MIIT and SAMR jointly issued the Notice on 25 February 2025. TÜV says it was published on February 28, 2025, and it will be effective immediately. Digital Policy Alert also gives 28 February as the entry-into-force date. The two dates differ, so check the official text before relying on either.
- **Filing duty:** Automakers must file their OTA upgrades with MIIT through its online software upgrade filing system, and with SAMR through its recall and safety data platform. SAMR reviews these filings and inspects OTA methods to stop manufacturers from hiding defects through updates (CMS, Law-Now, 17 March 2025).
- **Pre-approval for key changes:** Per Digital Policy Alert's summary, OTA updates that affect essential vehicle functions must be registered and approved before rollout. If an OTA is used for defect rectification or a recall, sales and production of the affected model must stop until corrective measures are approved (Digital Policy Alert).
- **OTA as recall:** Per 42how's reporting, an OTA upgrade used to eliminate a product defect counts as a form of recall, and a failed or defect-causing OTA requires a new recall.
- **Other obligations:** The Notice requires testing and reporting on safety features, a sandbox monitoring system, and reporting of vehicle-related incidents. Penalties apply for false reporting (Digital Policy Alert).
- **Deadlines:** Companies with already-approved ICVs had to submit supplementary technical data by 1 June 2025 (per Just Auto).

I did not find any 2026 implementing rules, amendments, or enforcement updates in this search. Searching the MIIT or SAMR websites directly for 2026 notices would be the next step.

Digital Policy Alert also gives 28 February as the entry-into-force date. The two dates differ, so check the official text before relying on either.
- **Filing duty:** Automakers must file their OTA upgrades with MIIT through its online software upgrade filing system, and with SAMR through its recall and safety data platform. SAMR reviews these filings and inspects OTA methods to stop manufacturers from hiding defects through updates (CMS, Law-Now, 17 March 2025).
- **Pre-approval for key changes:** Per Digital Policy Alert's summary, OTA updates that affect essential vehicle functions must be registered and approved before rollout. If an OTA is used for defect rectification or a recall, sales and production of the affected model must stop until corrective measures are approved (Digital Policy Alert).
- **OTA as recall:** Per 42how's reporting, an OTA upgrade used to eliminate a product defect counts as a form of recall, and a failed or defect-causing OTA requires a new recall.
- **Other obligations:** The Notice requires testing and reporting on safety features, a sandbox monitoring system, and reporting of vehicle-related incidents. Penalties apply for false reporting (Digital Policy Alert).
- **Deadlines:** Companies with already-approved ICVs had to submit supplementary technical data by 1 June 2025 (per Just Auto).

I did not find any 2026 implementing rules, amendments, or enforcement updates in this search. Searching the MIIT or SAMR websites directly for 2026 notices would be the next step.

content.content:
**Published:** 26 November 2025, effective in 2026.

**Physical controls and HMI**
- The HMI assessment checks the placement, clarity, and ease of use of essential controls, including "the availability of physical buttons for commonly used functions."
- Euro NCAP cites consumer feedback that physical buttons can reduce distraction.

**Driver monitoring**
- Euro NCAP will put more emphasis on driver monitoring, focusing on reliability and user acceptance.
- Top ratings require "continuous eye- and head-tracking" plus a link between driver-state data and driver assistance sensitivity.
- Extra credit goes to systems that detect drug or alcohol impairment and can safely stop the car if the driver becomes unresponsive.

**Driver assistance annoyance**
- Systems criticised for "annoying warnings or intrusive interventions" will be tested on real-world driving as well as on the track.
- Smoothness and intuitiveness in everyday driving, especially for lane support, will count toward scoring.

**Speed assist / ISA**
- The article does not mention speed assist or Intelligent Speed Assistance by name. It states that "verification of speed-limit information accuracy will be conducted during on-road driving tests" for the first time.

**Other customer-facing changes**
- Seatbelt-use detection and restraint optimisation for different body sizes earn higher scores.
- Pedal misapplication mitigation is rewarded under new low-speed collision tests.
- Electrically powered exterior door handles must stay operable after an impact.
- Automated emergency notifications must report the number of occupants, even when seatbelts are unfastened.
- EVs must warn the driver in a timely manner about battery-fire risk after a crash or during charging.

This document is intended to provide guidance to the Test Laboratory at the time of evaluating
the Euro NCAP Driver Controls assessment, as part of the Driver Engagement protocol.

Euro NCAP
Version 1.1 — October 2025

3

 1 TEST PROCEDURE
The Driver Controls assessment will be conducted by the test laboratory. The Vehicle
Manufacturer shall supply to Euro NCAP and the test laboratory a simple dossier containing
background information on the location, purpose and basic operation principle of controls for each
of the actions/tasks contained in this assessment.

Test vehicle
The assessment shall be conducted on a vehicle in its factory settings condition.
Individual/programmable settings (e.g., favorite buttons, shortcuts) shall not be assessed.
The assessment shall be conducted on a standstill condition, unless driving is required to assess
a specific function.
For the assessment of voice commands and media, the vehicle shall be in online condition, and
connected to a streaming service account.

Measurements
The entire assessment shall be recorded, for both transparency and for possible discussion
afterwards. The audiovisual recording shall capture the driver and the vehicle cockpit so that each
of the activated controls and the associated visual feedback can be seen.
-

Adjust the resolution and exposure to the light levels to ensure that the HMI can be
clearly identified.

remarks. For each row, the Test Laboratory will fill the following columns as indicated below:

The search confirms the basic timeline, with one nuance on scope.

- **Sept 12, 2025:** Most of the Data Act applies from this date. The obligations introduced under the EU's Data Act (Regulation 2023/2854) became applicable, including those related to connected products.
- **Sept 12, 2026:** The design obligation starts. Sources describe it as requiring connected products to make user data directly accessible where relevant and technically feasible. Under the Act's terms, Article 50 defers the design obligation in Article 3(1) so that it bites specifically on products first placed on the market after the 2026 date.
- **Scope for vehicles:** Sources say the duty covers connected vehicles. One source notes that a 'connected product' has a broad definition and can include smart appliances, machinery, and connected vehicles.

The main point to check is that the duty is tied to placing on the market, not to the calendar date alone. Vehicles already sold before September 2026 appear to fall outside the design duty, though the separate user access and sharing rights from September 2025 still apply to them. I did not find a source that addresses that split for vehicles explicitly, so confirm it against the regulation text (Articles 3 and 50) or an automotive-specific legal analysis before relying on it.

The search confirmed the regulation's dates but did not turn up the battery or brake figures you listed.

**Confirmed:**
- Regulation (EU) 2024/1257 entered into force on 28 May 2024, and the EUR-Lex summary describes it as tightening rules on exhaust pollutants and brake emissions. It also covers battery durability. (Implementation deadlines are phased in by vehicle category.)
- Application to new types of cars and vans starts on 29 November 2026. Application to all new cars and vans starts on 29 November 2027. (Heavy-duty dates are 29 May 2028 for new types and 29 May 2029 for new vehicles.)
- Brake particle requirements are part of the scope. Sources say the regulation expands EU vehicle emissions regulation beyond exhaust pollutants to include brake particle emissions, tire abrasion, and battery durability requirements for electric vehicles.

**Not confirmed:**
- None of the results gave the 80% state-of-health threshold, the 5-year or 100,000 km durability period, or the 72% brake particle reduction. Please check the Official Journal text or the Annex-level implementing acts for those numbers.
- One source notes that the regulation remains the subject of ongoing technical implementation work, including additional implementing acts and UNECE harmonization efforts covering testing methodologies, brake emissions, tire abrasion, and battery durability procedures. So the brake and battery test details may still be changing.

The search confirms the February 2027 deadline and the QR code requirement, and it gives a useful detail on state-of-health data.

- **Scope and deadline:** Sources agree that from 18 February 2027, EV, light-transport (LMT), and industrial batteries above 2 kWh need a battery passport. One source adds that the passport must be registered in the EU digital product passport registry before the battery is placed on the market, and that this registry went live on July 20, 2026. It applies under Article 77 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542. A QR code on the battery opens the passport, and its unique identifier must be registered in the EU digital product passport registry.
- **QR code scope:** One source says the QR code requirement covers all batteries, not only the large categories. From this date, all batteries must be marked with a QR code. Another says the QR code applies to the same date, with the full passport tied to the larger categories. A printed Article 13 label is required from 18 August 2026, and from 18 February 2027 the same battery must also carry a QR code under Article 13(6).
- **State of health:** The passport separates model-level and unit-level data. One source notes it holds model data, such as chemistry and hazardous substances, and individual data, such as state of health and status. Another says the public portion is limited, since not all information contained in the Battery Passport will be publicly accessible.
- **Responsibility:** The economic operator placing the battery on the market, normally the EU manufacturer or importer, is responsible for its content.

**Caveat:** A July 2026 commentary argues for keeping the passport but moving the date, so the February 2027 deadline may still be debated. I found no confirmed postponement. The sources also disagree on the entry-into-force date: most say 17 August 2023 and general application from 18 February 2024, but one says 18 February 2024 for entry into force.

Links: [{"title":"Artikel 5 VO (EU) 2023/1804","url":"https://gesetze.legal/eu/vo_eu_2023_1804/5"},{"title":"Image: Jucr","url":"https://www.electrive.com/2024/01/17/european-alternate-fuels-infrastructure-regulation-to-kick-in-from-april-13"},{"title":"a new mandatory legal framework for charging infrastructure in europe afir comes into force eu wide and eu commission publishes qa","url":"https://www.noerr.com/en/insights/a-new-mandatory-legal-framework-for-charging-infrastructure-in-europe-afir-comes-into-force-eu-wide-and-eu-commission-publishes-qa"},{"title":"ad hoc charging","url":"https://www.chargecloud.de/en-de/blog/ad-hoc-charging"},{"title":"AFIR: How can EV charge point operators comply with the EU’s ad-hoc payment requirements?","url":"https://blog.se.com/infrastructure-and-grid/automotive-mobility/2024/04/30/afir-how-can-ev-charge-point-operators-comply-with-the-eus-new-payment-requirements/"},{"title":"EU Regulation AFIR","url":"https://www.keba.com/en/news/emobility/blog-afir-what-it-means"},{"title":"Guide to AFIR for European charging businesses","url":"https://www.e-flux.io/blog/guide-afir-european-charging-businesses"},{"title":"reev integrates ev pay future proof card payment directly at the charging station","url":"https://reev.com/en/press/reev-integrates-ev-pay-future-proof-card-payment-directly-at-the-charging-station/"},{"title":"guide afir european charging businesses","url":"https://www.e-flux.io/en/blog/guide-afir-european-charging-businesses"},{"title":"The Global Coil Winding And Electrical Manufacturing Event","url":"https://berlin.cwiemeevents.com/articles/afir-comes-into-force"}]

The search turned up consistent answers on most of the points, with one scope discrepancy on the 2027 deadline.

- **Card readers at 50 kW and above:** Operators of new publicly accessible DC chargers of 50 kW or more deployed from 13 April 2024 must offer ad hoc payment through a payment card reader or a contactless device that can at least read cards. Newly built charging points with a power output of 50 kW or more must be equipped with either a payment card reader or a device with a contactless function that is at least able to read payment cards. QR codes do not satisfy this for DC units. Payment via QR code is excluded. Sub-50 kW units may use a dynamic QR code instead. For charging stations with lower charging capacities, a dynamic QR code is sufficient – but "dynamic" is the keyword here.

- **Price per kWh:** Article 5 of the regulation (German text) requires operators of 50 kW-plus points to display the ad hoc price per kWh, with any per-minute fees shown separately, at the station before charging starts. Operators of publicly accessible charging points with a charging capacity of 50 kW or more must display the ad hoc price per kWh and any usage fees as per-minute prices at the stations. The price components must appear in a set order: per kWh, per minute, per session, then anything else. The applicable price components shall be presented in the following order: Price per kilowatt-hour; price per minute; price per session; and any other price component that applies.

- **Existing chargers and the 2027 deadline:** Older units are not covered at first, but the obligation extends to them. From 1 Jan 2027 the ad hoc charging obligation is applicable to all public charge points of 50 kW or more, regardless of when they were deployed. Sources differ on scope. Noerr says the retrofit covers units along the TEN-T road network or in a safe and secure parking area, while e-flux describes it as applying to all 50 kW-plus points. I could not resolve this from the results. The regulation text should be checked for the exact scope.

The results did not include the full English text of Article 5's price provisions, so the pricing details rest on the German text and secondary summaries.

The search turned up no confirmation of a rule change after April 2026, so the September 1, 2029 deadline appears to stand, but it is in legal limbo.

- **Original rule and deadline:** In May 2024, NHTSA issued FMVSS 127, which establishes performance requirements for automatic emergency braking systems for light vehicles, with a deadline of September 1, 2029. The rule covers AEB, pedestrian AEB, and forward collision warning on all new passenger cars and light trucks weighing 10,000 pounds or less.
- **November 2024 revision:** NHTSA reviewed industry petitions for reconsideration and in November 2024 issued a revised final rule that granted portions of these petitions but left FMVSS 127 largely unchanged.
- **Current status (April 2026):** A Nelson Mullins analysis dated April 22, 2026 says subsequent regulatory action, litigation, and a freeze imposed by the Trump Administration have left automakers in limbo as to whether and when this rule will take effect and in what form. It adds that without some action, the September 2029 deadline set by NHTSA looms large.
- **Q1 2026 snapshot:** A VBOX Automotive whitepaper says the rule is the subject of active litigation in the US Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit and a regulatory amendment freeze under the current administration. It also states the compliance deadline has not moved.

Caveat: both sources are from early 2026 and I found nothing newer. Check the Federal Register and the D.C. Circuit docket for any developments after April 2026.

The Commission adopted the Automotive Package on 16 December 2025, and the search results agree on its main car CO2 change: the 2035 target moves from 100% to 90%. (One outlet, DieselNet, dates the release to 17 December.)

**Key points on the 2035 cars target:**
- The fleet-wide cut relative to 2021 falls from 100% to 90%. The remaining 10% to be offset through capped credits for alternative driver trains, sustainable renewable fuels, and use of low-carbon steel made in Europe.
- Plug-in hybrids, range extenders, mild hybrids and combustion-engine cars could still be sold after 2035 alongside battery-electric and hydrogen vehicles. This approach allows plug-in hybrids, range extenders, mild hybrids, and internal combustion engine vehicles to contribute alongside battery-electric and hydrogen vehicles beyond 2035.

**Other elements:**
- Interim flexibility: Between 2030-2032, a "banking and borrowing" scheme will be available to provide manufacturers with more flexibility in meeting 2030 targets for cars and vans.
- Vans: the 2030 target is reduced from 50% to 40%, per the Commission also proposes specific relief for the vans segment, where electrification has proven more challenging.
- Small EVs: The package introduces a new vehicle category for small electric vehicles up to 4.2 metres in length, and manufacturers could earn "super-credits" for building them in the EU.
- Corporate fleets: The package also sets binding national targets for corporate fleets.
- Battery Booster: It introduces the Battery Booster, allocating €1.8 billion to develop an EU-made battery value chain.

**Context:** The change follows industry and member-state pressure. Industry stakeholders and some member states increasingly have vocalized concerns about the achievability of these targets, especially given the slower than expected uptake of zero-emission vehicles. These are Commission proposals, so they still need to pass through the European Parliament and Council before taking effect. The EC submitted its proposals for the automotive sector to the European Parliament.

Porsche's petrol Macan and 718 Boxster/Cayman were pulled from European sales because of UN R155, which took effect on July 1, 2024. I ran one search, and the results are mostly trade-press articles rather than primary regulatory or Porsche sources.

- **The Macan:** Porsche decided at the end of 2023 to phase out the combustion Macan in the EU. A company spokesperson stated that only one-third of Macan sales come from the EU, while the US and China markets cover the remaining two-thirds. Porsche's electric Macan was planned as the replacement.
- **The 718:** Porsche later confirmed the same rule would end sales of the 718 pair in Europe. The Cayman GT4 RS and Boxster Spyder RS will be able to skirt the rule given their limited production volume. One source says there is no hard deadline for the sports cars.
- **Why R155 bites:** Porsche said that compliance would mean redeveloping the electrical architecture, which is costly and slow. The UN R155 regulation requires vehicles to have an anti-hacking management system (CSMS) to ensure that practices and measures are adequately applied across the development process and life cycle of vehicles.
- **Timing:** One source describes the rules as in effect since July 2022 for new series launched on the market and will apply to all new vehicles manufactured from July 2024 onwards.

Caveats: the sources are secondary reporting from early 2024 and don't confirm current sales status. I didn't find a primary Porsche or UNECE statement, so check those before relying on the details.

The EU's General Safety Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 applied to all new vehicles sold from 7 July 2024, and the rules were already in force for new vehicle types from July 2022.

- **Scope and timing:** The Commission says new rules on general vehicle safety now apply to all new motor vehicles sold in the EU as of 7 July 2024. Its fact sheet adds that measures are being progressively introduced between July 2024 to January 2029.
- **Systems required:** All new motor vehicles, including cars, vans, trucks, and buses must include intelligent speed assistance, reversing detection, drowsiness attention warnings, and an emergency stop signal. Cars and vans also need lane keeping, automated braking, and event data recorders.
- **Switching off ISA:** The regulation text says it shall be possible to switch off the system, but ISA must return to normal operation upon each activation of the vehicle master control switch. Speed-limit information may still be shown while it is off.
- **Drowsiness warning:** The Commission's delegated act describes a system that shall monitor a driver's level of drowsiness and alert the driver through the vehicle human machine interface. The Commission justifies this by noting that driver fatigue is a factor in 10-25 % of all road crashes in the Union.
- **Expected impact:** The Commission expects these measures to help save over 25,000 lives and avoid at least 140,000 serious injuries by 2038.

Sources are mainly official EU pages (Commission press release dated 5 July 2024, the Commission fact sheet, and the consolidated EUR-Lex text), plus an EU Urban Mobility Observatory article from 2022. The search didn't turn up any dispute over these dates.

**Publish date:** 23 December 2025. The Commission put the package forward on 16 December 2025.

**2035 target (100% to 90%):** From 2035, M1 and N1 manufacturers must meet an "emissions reduction target of 90%" (currently 100%). The remaining 10% can be offset through EU-made low-carbon steel, e-fuels, or biofuels, via "fuel credits."

**2025–2027 averaging:** The EU already allowed some flexibility, requiring that "the overall average emission target needs to be met for the years 2025 to 2027."

**2030 target:** The article gives no specific 2030 percentage. It says "an overall assessment is to apply for the period between 2030 and 2032" and that the van CO2 target will be "slightly reduced for the years between 2030 and 2034."

**Status:** Proposal only. The article says the proposed regulations "will now have to go through the EU legislative process," and that the final changes remain open given industry criticism.

**PHEV/range extender after 2035:** The article says the fuel-credit approach is "intended to ensure the future viability of hybrid vehicles (plug-in hybrids, range extenders, mild hybrids)." It makes no further statement on these vehicles after 2035.

**Publish date:** April 22, 2026, by Bridget E. Harris, Alexis D. Cheatum, and Colin A. Brown of Nelson Mullins.

**Key requirements (FMVSS 127):** The rule applies to new passenger cars and light trucks weighing 10,000 pounds or less. Vehicles must be capable of:
- **Speeds and lead-vehicle avoidance:** "full collision avoidance with a lead vehicle" at speeds up to 62 mph.
- **Braking speeds:** Automatic braking engages up to 90 mph for imminent vehicle collisions, and up to 45 mph when a pedestrian is detected.
- **Pedestrians and night:** Systems must "detect pedestrians in both daylight and darkness."

**Deadline:** Most manufacturers must have the required crash mitigation features in place by September 1, 2029. Small-volume manufacturers, final-stage manufacturers, and alterers have until September 1, 2030.

**Status and limbo:**
- NHTSA issued the rule in May 2024 and a revised final rule in November 2024, which granted some industry petitions but left the rule largely unchanged.
- In January 2025, Auto Innovators challenged the rule in the D.C. Circuit. Days later, the new administration's regulatory freeze took effect, and the DOT moved to hold the case in abeyance. The case has remained paused since.
- On March 23, 2026, the DOT told the court it is preparing a proposed rule to amend parts of FMVSS 127. The proposal would give manufacturers two more years, to provide "more time to achieve challenging aspects of the standard."
- Unless that change is adopted, the September 2029 deadline still applies. The article concludes that automakers face continued uncertainty about their near-term obligations.

The search results confirm the core termination, with a few details relevant to leased EVs.

One source says the New Clean Vehicle Credit (30D) and Qualified Commercial Clean Vehicle Credit (45W) were both eliminated on 30 September 2025, and another notes that the 25E used-vehicle credit ended on that date too.
- **Legal basis:** The termination came from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, enacted as Public Law 119-21 on July 4, 2025. One source places it in OBBBA Section 70503 for 45W, which it describes as covering vehicles acquired after that date.

- **Current status:** One source states that for most buyers in 2026, there is no federal purchase credit.

The sources are mostly secondary (industry sites and a tax-guidance site), and one quotes the statute directly. I did not verify the statutory text against the Code itself, so check IRS guidance or Form 8936 instructions before relying on the grandfathering rules for a specific transaction.

The search confirms the core policy: the 2026–2027 NEV purchase tax is halved, with a per-vehicle cap of 15,000 yuan. The MIIT technical thresholds are also tighter, most notably for plug-in hybrids.

**Tax terms:** Full exemption ran for NEVs bought in 2024–2025, capped at 30,000 yuan per vehicle. For purchases from January 1, 2026 through December 31, 2027, the tax is halved, with the reduction capped at 15,000 yuan per passenger car (NEVs purchased from Jan. 1, 2024, to Dec. 31, 2025 will be exempted from vehicle purchase tax. The tax exemption amount for each new energy passenger vehicle will not exceed 30,000 yuan. From January 1, 2026, to December 31, 2027, new energy vehicles purchased will be subject to a halved vehicle purchase tax, with a tax reduction amount for each NEPV not exceeding 15,000 yuan.). The standard rate is 10%, so the effective rate becomes 5% (the standard purchase tax in China for all vehicles at the time of registration is 10 percent of the vehicle invoice price). The announcement was issued jointly by the Ministry of Finance, the State Taxation Administration and MIIT (China will extend its preferential purchase tax policy for NEVs to the end of 2027).

**Technical requirements:** Eligibility covers pure electric, plug-in hybrid (including extended-range) and fuel-cell vehicles that meet NEV technical requirements (the NEVs eligible for the vehicle purchase tax exemption policy refer to pure electric vehicles, plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (including extended-range models), and fuel cell vehicles that meet the technical requirements for NEVs). The biggest change is for PHEVs: the pure-electric range minimum rises from 43 km to 100 km. Energy and fuel-consumption limits are also tightened by vehicle weight, under the GB 36980.1-2025 standard, which also sets stricter efficiency benchmarks for battery-electric cars (Plug-in hybrids must have a minimum 100 km of pure-electric range, up from 43 km, while energy and fuel-consumption limits are tightened according to vehicle weight. The policy will apply under the GB 36980.1-2025 national standard).

**Caveats:** The 200 km BEV range and battery-density figures in the ETN article date from the 2024 rule set, so check the current MIIT catalog before relying on them. One analyst estimate (Huayuan Securities) says roughly 40% of PHEV/EREVs may lose subsidies under the stricter range rule. That is a forecast, not an official figure.

- **Vehicle type:** The rule "applies only to passenger vehicles," defined as those under 10,001 pounds. Commercial vehicles are excluded for now.

The search didn't turn up a 2026 draft mandatory GB standard on in-car cameras or personal information. What it did surface is the surrounding regulatory framework, which is related but not the specific document you asked about.

- **GB/T 44464-2024 (recommended, not mandatory):** SAC/TC114 released this standard in August 2024. It covers general requirements for data generated and collected during vehicle research, design, and manufacturing, including personal information protection and key data protection. For key data, vehicles must set parameters for cameras, radar, and other equipment according to the precision needs of functional services. It also points to GB 44495-2024 for cybersecurity of data storage and transfer.

- **2026 cross-border guidance:** On 3 February 2026, MIIT and CAC, with six other agencies, published the Guidance for the Secure Cross-Border Transfer of Automotive Data (2026 Edition). It sets out specific standards for identifying important data across five contexts and nine sub-contexts. Notably, "personal data of more than 100,000 data subjects" is no longer identified as important data per se under the new guidance.

- **Underlying rules:** The Automobile Data Security provisions took effect on 1 October 2021, and the important data category has included video and image data outside vehicles that contains facial information and license plate information. The 2025 effective date appears in a later source: the Network Data Security Management Regulations came into effect on 1 January 2025.

The search confirms the core facts, though the sources differ on some timing details.

- **Formal notice:** Commerce and USTR published a Federal Register notice on September 24, 2025 amending the tariff schedule to implement the framework agreement. Reuters reported that it set the 15% rate for EU autos and auto parts as of August 1. Butzel's client alert dates the publication to September 25, 2025.
- **Legal basis:** Total tariffs on EU autos and parts covered by Section 232 duties under Proclamation 10908 are 15% or the MFN rate, whichever is greater. The change is retroactive to August 1, 2025. Executive Order 14346, issued September 5, 2025, authorized the tariff modifications.
- **Calculation method:** One law-firm summary says for goods with a Column 1 duty rate at or below 15%, the Section 232 rate is 15% minus the Column 1 rate.
- **Conditionality and timing:** Bloomberg (via CPA Practice Advisor) reported that the relief for automobiles and parts was contingent on the EU introducing legislation to lower tariffs on American industrial goods. Other coverage describes the reduction as taking effect from the start of the month in which the EU introduces its proposal, which is a different trigger from the August 1 date.
- **Exemptions:** Reuters reported that the notice exempts all aircraft and aircraft parts, and generic pharmaceuticals and their ingredients and chemical precursors. Butzel says the reciprocal-tariff elimination for these items is retroactive to September 1, 2025.
- **Refunds:** Companies can claim retroactive tariff refunds by submitting Post-Summary Corrections.

I did not check the Federal Register itself, so the notice citation and the effective-date details rest on secondary reporting. A search for the notice number or the Federal Register document would confirm the exact dates and conditions.
