The search turned up good coverage of the 2021 draft and the 2025–2026 follow-on guidance, but nothing on the "default not collect" cabin-data rule, so that part is unverified.

**2021 draft (CAC):** The CAC issued the draft automotive data security provisions in May 2021 for public comment. They aim to regulate the collection, analysis, storage, utilization, and export of personal information and important data generated over a vehicle's lifecycle. Article 12 of the draft would require personal information and important data to be stored within China, and an Operator needing to send such data abroad would have to undergo a cross-border security assessment organized by the CAC. It was the first time a Chinese ministerial department issued data security management rules for the automotive industry.

**Final rules and later guidance:** The search results don't confirm the status of the final 2021 rules. Their effective date and whether the cabin-default provision survived are from my own memory, not these sources, and should be checked. The results do cover later developments:
- On June 13, 2025, China released draft guidelines for exporting automotive data generated within its borders, jointly issued by eight agencies. They are the most detailed effort to date to define and restrict "important data" in the auto sector. The draft identifies 49 types of automotive data across five categories as potentially "important" and subject to review.
- On February 3, 2026, MIIT and seven other authorities released the Security Guidelines on Cross-Border Automobile Data Transfers (2026 Edition). For the first time they systematically define important automotive data and set out transfer pathways across six scenarios.

**Not found:** Nothing in these results addresses the cabin-data default (that in-vehicle data is not collected or processed outside the vehicle unless needed). A follow-up search on in-vehicle processing principles would be needed to confirm it.

- **Phase 2 scope:** A UNECE achievements page lists R171 DCAS "Phase 2" as hands-off, eyes-on system-initiated manoeuvres on motorways (171 (DCAS) - Phase 1 - Hands on) - Phase 2 - Hands off / Eyes on / System Initiated Manoeuvres on motorways.)
- **Adoption:** A UNECE working-party page says that June 2026 WP.29 adopted the 02 series of amendments to UN Regulation No. 171 (DCAS). Treat this as the key adoption signal, but I could not check it against WP.29's official report.
- **Earlier 01 series:** A 2024 UNECE wiki record shows the 01 series draft limited system-initiated manoeuvres to highways (restricts performing system-initiated manoeuvres on highways only.). That draft was then reworked.
- **02 series content:** A January 2026 GRVA informal document proposes the 02 series, including special provisions for system-initiated manoeuvres in non-highway environments or while hands-on requests are withheld (Special provisions for systems capable of performing system-initiated manoeuvres in non-highway environments or during phases of withholding of HORs.). A later GRVA draft carries the same structure and adds controllability requirements for those cases.
- **Gaps:** The results do not state the entry-into-force date, transition periods, or the final adopted text. The search metadata ages are inconsistent, so I'd verify dates against the UNECE WP.29 session reports or the official R171 document before relying on them. The 2025 and 2026 timing in your query is only partly confirmed.

Links: [{"title":"finitestate.io","url":"https://finitestate.io/hubfs/Collateral/GB%20Standards%20data%20sheet.pdf"},{"title":"Chinese Automated Driving Standards","url":"https://newlypossible.org/wiki/Chinese_Automated_Driving_Standards"},{"title":"sesec.eu","url":"https://sesec.eu/?p=2746"},{"title":"automotive cybersecurity regulations and standards","url":"https://diconium.com/en/blog/cybersecurity/automotive-cybersecurity-regulations-and-standards"},{"title":"sesec.eu","url":"https://sesec.eu/?p=8091"},{"title":"Automotive Cybersecurity Regulations and Standards","url":"https://diconium.com/en/blog/automotive-cybersecurity-regulations-and-standards"},{"title":"GB44496 2024","url":"https://www.chinesestandard.net/PDF_MS.aspx/GB44496-2024"},{"title":"sesec.eu","url":"https://sesec.eu/tag/software/"},{"title":"GB44495 2024","url":"https://www.chinesestandard.net/PDF_MS.aspx/GB44495-2024"},{"title":"GB 44495-2024 PDF English","url":"https://www.chinesestandard.net/PDF.aspx/GB44495-2024"}]

The search doesn't support the January 2027 date for all vehicles. The sources I found give different timelines, and one indicates the rules were amended in 2026.

- **Original dates:** The standards were issued in August 2024 with an effective date of January 1, 2026. The three mandatory national standards were issued by the Standardization Administration of China, and they were set to take effect on January 1, 2026.
- **Software-update transition (GB 44496):** One vendor summary says the software-update standard applies to new type approvals from January 1, 2026, and to existing types by January 1, 2028 (GB 44496-2024 (software update) enforced for new type approvals from Jan 1, 2026, and for existing types by Jan 1, 2028). This is the only source I found with a 2028 deadline, and it conflicts with your January 2027 premise.
- **Amendment No. 1:** A wiki page reports that Amendment No. 1 to GB 44495 and GB 44496 was approved and took effect on 28 January 2026, limiting the applicable vehicles to M and N categories and providing that the two standards apply to vehicle types newly applying for type approval from 1 July 2026. That would change the timeline significantly, but I couldn't confirm it against an official notice.
- **Scope:** One source says GB 44495 applies to vehicles in categories M and N, as well as category O vehicles equipped with at least one electronic control unit. Another says GB 44496 applies to M, N, and O category vehicles capable of software updates. The amendment reportedly narrowed the scope to M and N, so the sources disagree on which categories are covered.

Based on these results, the January 2027 "all vehicles" date is unverified. The most consistent picture is January 2026 for new type approvals under the original text, with later transition dates that depend on whether Amendment No. 1 applies. Check the official SAMR/MIIT notices or the amendment text before relying on any specific deadline.

**Publish date:** The guidance was issued on 3 February 2026. The DLA Piper article was published on 4 February 2026.

**Issuing agencies:** The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), the sectoral regulator, and the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC), the designated data regulator, issued it together with six other government authorities.

**What auto data counts as important data:**
- **Location:** Under vehicle-road perception, the article lists "location trajectories, inertial navigation data, autonomous driving maps" as covered data.
- **Charging:** Under V2X platform operation, it lists "network planning, charging operation, and security assurance data."
- **Cabin video:** The article does not mention cabin video.
- The guidance no longer treats "personal data of more than 100,000 data subjects" as important data per se.

**Consequences for cross-border transfer:**
- Controllers do not need to sign or file China SCCs or obtain CAC approval for three categories of personal data: security vulnerability data, security incident data, and OTA source code. This applies only where the data "does not otherwise constitute important data."
- Other personal data transfers remain subject to the existing rules.
- Controllers must designate responsible staff, set internal approval procedures, and keep detailed transfer logs. "Detailed transfer logs must be retained for at least three years."
- Controllers must also meet encryption requirements in transit and keep samples of outbound network traffic.
- Controllers must compile their own important data catalogues and submit them to authorities, though the article says the process is not yet explained.
- The authors expect local authorities to enforce these requirements more strictly.

The search results support the 02 series amendment to UN R171, but none of them confirm the final WP.29 vote.

- **Proposal:** The draft 02 series would delete the rule that DCAS may start a manoeuvre only on a highway and not while withholding hands-on requests. It would add special test provisions for systems that initiate manoeuvres in non-highway settings or while hands-on requests are withheld. The previous requirement that the "system shall only initiate a manoeuvre if the vehicle is located on a highway and it is not withholding HORs" has been entirely deleted. Conversely, "test scenarios" for "systems capable of performing system-initiated manoeuvres in non-highway environments or during phases of withholding HORs" have been added as special provisions.
- **Committee stage:** A 02 series of amendments to UN R171 (GRVA-24-17/Rev.2) was approved and submitted to WP.29 as WP.29/2026/86. GRVA adopted the draft and asked for a consideration and vote at their June 2026 sessions.
- **Dissent:** Norway voiced reservations, arguing that the extensions given to hands off situations and system-initiated manoeuvres may make DCAS too close to ADS.
- **Outcome unconfirmed:** One blog post describes the amendment as expected to be adopted at the UN WP.29 World Forum starting next week on June 23, 2026, but it is a forecast written before the vote. I found no report of the actual result, so treat adoption as unverified. Also, the results do not explicitly tie this to European motorway hands-free driving, so that link is inference.

Links: [{"title":"automotivespin.isti.cnr.it 19w lomi 2","url":"https://automotivespin.isti.cnr.it/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/automotivespin.isti.cnr.it-19w-lomi-2.pdf"},{"title":"Zum Inhalt springen","url":"https://www.ki-syndikat.de/usecases/automotive/15-ota-update-management/"},{"title":"software update management system sums","url":"https://ul.com/sis/resources/software-update-management-system-sums"},{"title":"Kai Frederik ZASTROW STELLANTIS V2","url":"https://fnc.itu.int/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/Kai-Frederik-ZASTROW-STELLANTIS-V2.pdf"},{"title":"software update management system sums","url":"https://www.ul.com/de/sis/resources/software-update-management-system-sums"},{"title":"Haldex | What is R156?","url":"https://www.haldex.com/en/europe/trailer-application-guide/sums/r156/what/"},{"title":"atlantis-press.com","url":"https://atlantis-press.com/article/126000242.pdf"},{"title":"Trusted Software POV Software Update Management","url":"https://www.deloitte.com/content/dam/Deloitte/de/Documents/risk/Trusted-Software-POV-Software-Update-Management.pdf"},{"title":"unece r156","url":"https://www.itemis.com/en/glossary/unece-r156/"}]

Under UN R156, the July 2024 milestone applies to all newly produced and sold vehicles, but sources disagree on the exact dates and on what it means for customers.

**Timing:** The main sources give the same basic schedule. One says since July 2022 mandatory for all new vehicle types, and since July 2024 mandatory for all newly produced and sold vehicles, including existing types. The EU anchors these deadlines in the General Safety Regulation (EU) 2019/2144. Haldex gives a different EU timetable: July 2024 for new EU type approvals and from July 2026 for new registrations. Treat the registration date as unsettled until you check the official UNECE or EU texts.

**Customer-facing requirements:** R156 is mainly a manufacturer obligation, but it includes rules that affect owners. For over-the-air updates, the update must not compromise the safety of the vehicle while it is being performed, a failed update must lead to a safe state, and the vehicle user must be informed about the purpose and impact of the update. Haldex adds that R156 ensures that vehicles remain compliant with their initial type approval throughout their lifecycle.

**Consequences for OEMs:** A Software Update Management System becomes a prerequisite for type approval: the manufacturer must be able to prove at any time which software version runs on which vehicle type and whether an update affects the approval. Haldex notes that manufacturers must provide evidence to technical authorities for type approval, market surveillance, recalls, and periodic inspections.

**Caveat on penalties:** One German vendor page claims compliance penalties for UNECE-R156 violations of up to 200,000 euros per violation. I did not find this figure in an official source, so I would not rely on it. I also did not find any source describing a specific customer-facing consequence, such as warranty or recall changes, beyond the user-information and safety requirements above.

The standard is confirmed to take effect July 1, 2026, and it makes "no fire, no explosion" a mandatory requirement for traction batteries.

- **Effective date and scope:** Two mandatory national standards, GB 38031-2025 (traction batteries) and GB 18384-2025 (vehicle-level), take effect on July 1. This marks the first time in China's new energy vehicle sector that both battery-specific and vehicle-level core safety standards take effect on the same day.
- **The core change:** The battery standard replaces the earlier threshold. Under GB 38031-2020, a battery could avoid fire or explosion for a "5-minute buffer period" after thermal runaway. The new rule makes the no-fire, no-explosion outcome mandatory. Industry sources describe it as the world's first such requirement.
- **Added tests:** The standard adds two mandatory tests: bottom impact, simulating underbody strikes, and long-term fast-charging cycling.
- **Cost impact:** One market estimate cited by CnEVPost says meeting the new rules will raise battery system costs by 15% to 20%. Major makers such as CATL and Eve Energy say they already met the requirements years ago.

The draft was released by China's Ministry of Public Security in November 2025, and the 5-second rule applies only to the default start-up state, not to the car's peak performance.

- **The draft:** On November 10, the ministry released a consultation draft of the updated national standard "Technical Conditions for Motor Vehicle Operation Safety." The clause would apply to passenger vehicles and excludes automatic start-stop systems.
- **Default mode, not a hard cap:** Drivers could still pick a faster setting. One outlet notes that through operations similar to switching driving modes, users can lift the acceleration restriction after making an active choice.
- **Ministry clarification:** After online backlash over claims that fast EV acceleration would be banned, the ministry clarified that the draft does not restrict sub-five-second 0–100 km/h acceleration capabilities.
- **Interpretation caveat:** Electrive reads the term "default" the same way, saying it likely refers only to the default drive mode configured at vehicle startup. Carscoops describes the restriction as something that could work much like the output-limiting Eco setting found in most EVs.

Sources conflict on how much the rule changes things. Jiemian describes it as a requirement that has stirred debate across the EV industry. I found no final adopted version in these results, so the status is still a draft.

The February 2025 date in your query is the original start for certification, not the fire date. The fire was in August 2024, and the government moved certification up.

- **The fire:** On August 1, 2024, a Mercedes-Benz EQE caught fire in an underground garage in Incheon. The car had a Farasis Energy battery, and the blaze took eight hours to extinguish. It destroyed or damaged around 140 cars and forced apartment residents to relocate to shelters.
- **Certification:** The government and the ruling party moved the new battery certification program up to October, instead of February 2025, when it was originally due. Manufacturers must get approval from the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport confirming their batteries meet local safety standards. This had previously been voluntary.
- **Disclosure:** The government and the People Power Party agreed to require automakers to disclose the battery brand information for all EVs. Manufacturers would have to disclose capacity, maximum output, and base materials.
- **Industry response:** Hyundai listed battery makers for all its EV models on its Korean website, and Kia and BMW Korea followed. A Mercedes-Benz spokesperson said that if disclosure became mandatory, the company would comply. Mercedes-Benz Korea then released its battery supplier names.
- **Cause:** The exact cause, whether battery, battery management system, or external factors, was still under investigation in the sources I found.

Note that the results are from August 2024. I didn't check whether the October certification start actually happened on schedule, so the current status of the rules is unconfirmed.

The access-by-design obligation "applies to connected products and related services that are made available on the EU market after 12 September 2026." Under this rule, products should let users reach their data directly, where relevant and technically feasible.

Users "can ask a data holder to send their data to a third party, and it should happen without undue delay." Data provided to users should also be free of charge. The article does not mention repairers specifically. Repairers are an example of a third party that could receive data under this right.

- **Context:** Euro 7 also introduces an Environmental Vehicle Passport, which is intended to give used-EV buyers better visibility of battery health (each vehicle being issued an Environmental Vehicle Passport containing information on its environmental performance at the moment of registration.).

The search didn't confirm that the Commission has published a formal Digital Fairness Act proposal. The sources I found cover the consultation and the earlier Fitness Check, so check the Commission's site for the current status.

- **Background:** The Commission's Fitness Check found that 69% of consumers consulted experienced some kind of technical difficulty in cancelling their online contracts. Those problems included deliberate avoidance of cancellations, and websites/apps designed to introduce friction into the cancellation process.
- **Existing rules:** The Consumer Rights Directive gives a 14-day cooling-off period for online subscriptions, which starts when the subscription contract commences, even if it includes a free trial period. Under the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive, making it unreasonably difficult for consumers to cancel an online subscription may be a prohibited unfair practice. In the absence of harmonised EU rules, member states have their own cancellation requirements.
- **Proposed direction:** Commentary on the DFA says it will address subscription services that are very easy to sign up for and deliberately complicated to cancel, including automatic renewals and free trials that silently convert into paid subscriptions. The Commission is weighing requiring clear disclosure of subscription terms, mandating simple cancellation mechanisms ("cancel as easily as you subscribed"), and restricting certain upselling practices.
- **Timeline:** The consultation closed on 9 October 2025, and responses will feed into an Impact Assessment that forms part of the preparation of a DFA proposal. One June 2026 commentary notes that the scope of the DFA will only be clear once the proposal is published, which suggests the proposal was still pending at that point.

The search supports the July 2026 date, with one nuance about which vehicles it covers.

- **Date and scope:** A Smart Eye press release dated 7 July 2026 says ADDW systems are mandatory in all new vehicles sold on the European market under the EU's General Safety Regulation (GSR). It also says the requirement covers passenger cars, trucks, and buses.
- **What ADDW detects:** The systems aim to catch visual distraction, for example by looking away from the road, interacting with in-car systems, or using a mobile device.
- **Camera/driver monitoring:** The release says steering or lane-keeping data are generally not enough to detect visual distraction reliably. Compliant systems therefore need to assess the driver directly, typically using sensors and software capable of analyzing head and eye movements. That points to camera-based driver monitoring, though the release doesn't mandate a specific technology.
- **Timeline nuance:** Seeing Machines, a driver-monitoring vendor, describes a staged rollout. It says ADDW have been required in all new vehicle types within the European Union (EU) since July 2024, and that they will also become mandatory for all newly registered vehicles from July 2026. So the 2026 date applies to all registrations, while 2024 was the deadline for new vehicle types.
- **Source caveat:** The 2026 claims come from Smart Eye's own press release, a company that sells this technology. I didn't find an official EU regulation text in these results, so check the GSR (Regulation (EU) 2019/2144) and its implementing acts before relying on the exact scope or exemptions.

The C-NCAP 2027 edition was released in April 2026, and the search results have little detail on the 2024 edition's driver monitoring or assisted-driving scoring.

- **2027 edition release:** CATARC published the 2027 protocol in April 2026 at the C-NCAP 20th anniversary event. The anniversary event also set the direction for the future with the simultaneous release of the C-NCAP 2027 Edition Protocol. A draft had been published for public comment in February 2026. It was released as a draft for public consultation on February 12, 2026.
- **Changes to driver monitoring:** The official C-NCAP site lists the DMS changes against the 2024 edition. Its DMS section adds test scenarios for system intervention and false response. The same list also adjusts the minimum score rate requirements for star ratings and introduces requirements for physical control devices.
- **Overall impact:** CATARC expects scores to fall. Vehicles that meet the 2024 standards are expected to see overall scores drop by about 8 percent under the new protocol, and some models are likely to be downgraded by one star or more. The new edition also adds multiple test items for battery safety and advanced driver-assistance systems.
- **2024 edition:** Coverage is thin. A LeddarTech white paper says the 2024 protocol makes active safety, incorporating advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS), driver monitoring systems (DMS) and road feature recognition (RFR), a key element. It doesn't give the DMS scoring method.
- **Assisted-driving scoring:** I found no C-NCAP-specific assisted-driving scoring details. The results on assisted-driving grading are about Euro NCAP, which is a different program.

- **Earlier UK survey (2019):** A CLM Fleet Management survey of almost 300 UK motorists, run before the mandate, found 68% expected drivers to turn them off for every journey.
- **US survey (2024):** An IIHS survey of 1,802 American drivers found more than 60% of drivers would find it acceptable if their vehicle provided an audible and visual warning when they exceeded the posted speed limit. This is a US study, so it doesn't speak to EU drivers directly.

The results point to a Japanese driver-monitoring mandate tied to the UN WP.29 rules, plus a proposed UN R171 amendment that loosens hands-off limits. Some sources conflict on dates, and I couldn't confirm the final outcomes.

**Driver monitoring (DMS):** A August 2026 Jiji Press report says Japan's transport ministry plans to require DMS in both domestic and imported vehicles. The ministry plans to revise an ordinance in September to apply the new requirement to new models starting 2031 and existing models in 2033. Alerts trigger when a driver fails to look ahead for six seconds while going at speeds between 20 and 50 kilometers per hour, and for 3.5 seconds while going at speeds above 50 kph. A MarkLines piece says these rules align with international DMS regulations adopted at WP.29 in March 2026, though the article is paywalled and I couldn't verify the details.

**UN R171 (DCAS) hands-off:** A teskas.net post describes a proposed 02 series amendment expected to be voted on at WP.29 starting June 23, 2026. It deletes the earlier requirement that the system initiate a manoeuvre only on a highway while not withholding hands-on requests, and adds test scenarios for non-highway operation. A Global AutoRegs agenda from March 2026 lists related draft amendments, including new "highway-like road" definitions. I did not find confirmation that the June vote passed.

**Japan's domestic side:** A March 2026 MLIT working group meeting expected a conclusion... around the summer, and it appears to be waiting on the WP.29 revisions. An E2E AI driving-support function is expected to reach market in fiscal 2027 as a Level 2 feature.

**Older context:** An S&P Global article describes an earlier Japanese rule requiring an alarm roughly every 15 seconds when hands leave the wheel on a highway. It is undated in the results and likely predates the current rules.

Caveat: the sources conflict on timing. One source puts the DMS adoption at March 2026, and another describes the WP.29 vote as still upcoming in June. I'd verify against MLIT and UNECE primary documents before relying on specific dates.

The search results confirm the extension. In April 2023 the Commission prolonged the Motor Vehicle Block Exemption Regulation, so it now runs to 31 May 2028. The short extension is meant to let the Commission respond quickly to market shifts such as vehicle digitalisation, electrification and new mobility patterns.

On repair data access, the updated Supplementary Guidelines extend existing principles on technical information, tools and training to vehicle-generated data. Under Article 101 TFEU, authorised and independent repairers should be able to access such data on an equal footing. The guidelines also require vehicle suppliers to apply a proportionality principle when they consider withholding data on cybersecurity grounds. One guidance point treats a manufacturer's refusal to give independent operators vehicle-generated data as a potential abuse of a dominant position (the updated guidelines identify this as a potential abuse of a dominant position).

Industry reaction was mixed. FIGIEFA, the European aftermarket distributors' association, called the prolongation an important step in maintaining competition in the automotive aftermarket, but said some aspects will require further clarification.

The search confirms the September 1, 2027 date. The final rule amends FMVSS No. 208 to require a seat belt use warning for rear seats, and the compliance date for those rear-seat requirements is September 1, 2027, with optional early compliance allowed. Multi-stage manufacturers and alterers get one extra year. The front seat belt warning requirements have an earlier date of September 1, 2026 ([Federal Register](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-01-03/html/2024-30340.htm)). The rule was published January 3, 2025, at 90 FR 390, under docket NHTSA-2024-0071 ([GAO](https://gao.gov/assets/880/876163.pdf)).

The sources differ on the effective date. The Federal Register copy gives March 4, 2025 ([govinfo PDF](https://govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-01-03/pdf/2024-30340.pdf)), while a later J.J. Keller reproduction gives March 20, 2025 ([J.J. Keller](https://www.jjkellercompliancenetwork.com/news/details/JJ131169-L-1736263176889)). The compliance dates are the same in all of them.

I ran one search and did not check whether NHTSA has changed or delayed these dates since 2025.

Links: [{"title":"globalautoregs.com","url":"https://globalautoregs.com/agendas/13372"},{"title":"22-25 Apr | Geneva","url":"https://globalautoregs.com/agendas/13020"},{"title":"globalautoregs.com","url":"https://globalautoregs.com/meetings/3037?rule_id=59"},{"title":"Show admin view","url":"https://globalautoregs.com/documents/23867"},{"title":"22-25 Oct 2024 | Geneva","url":"https://globalautoregs.com/agendas/12538"},{"title":"globalautoregs.com","url":"https://globalautoregs.com/documents/28182"},{"title":"globalautoregs.com","url":"https://globalautoregs.com/documents/26804"},{"title":"globalautoregs.com","url":"https://globalautoregs.com/documents/20896"},{"title":"globalautoregs.com","url":"https://globalautoregs.com/documents/22115"}]

The search turned up UNECE GRE working documents, not a confirmed final rule, so I can't say from these results whether illuminated grille or logo lighting is currently permitted in Europe.

- **Background:** Since 2019, France and Germany have pushed for rules on logos inside lamp surfaces. One 2019 proposal, GRE-82-20, was to allow under specified conditions the use of manufacturer logos inside the illuminant surface of a signalling lamp. In 2020 GRE postponed the revised proposal to the next session, due to the ongoing work on the proposal, and reiterated its request to type approval authorities to refrain from granting type approvals to lamps with such logos.
- **2022–2023:** OICA proposed allowing logos smaller than 5 cm2, but a number of experts from contracting parties delivered critical remarks and were not in a position to support the proposal.
- **October 2025 session (GRE-93):** A German proposal aimed to clarify that only light-signalling devices may incorporate an illuminated manufacturer logo. OICA's GRE/2025/18 would prohibit the inclusion of a manufacturer logo in headlamps under UN R149 and limit the approval of light-signalling devices with a logo to the 01 series of amendment of UN R149 under UN R48. A related OICA package (GRE/2025/20) would add requirements for the implementation of a manufacturer logo under UN R149 and a corresponding provision under UN R48, and its status was listed as formal GR review in the agenda. The results don't show whether any of these were adopted.

Practical takeaway: the direction of travel appears to be that logos may be illuminated only within light-signalling devices (not headlamps), with limits tied to specific series of amendments. Check the current UNECE WP.29 adopted texts for R48 and R149, or the GRE session reports from late 2025 and 2026, to confirm what is in force.

The most recent reports say the House passed the bill, but I found no evidence that the Senate has passed it.

**House:** Reports from September 2026 say the House passed H.R. 979 on September 15, 2026, by voice vote under suspension of the rules. The bill directs the Department of Transportation and NHTSA to establish a rule making AM radio standard equipment in new passenger vehicles. The AP account describes the vote differently, saying it passed unanimously late Tuesday, which is consistent with a voice vote.

**Senate:** The companion bill is S. 315. One AP report says the Senate is considering a similar measure. I found no report of Senate floor passage.

**Conflicting reports:** Some earlier coverage says the bill had not reached a floor vote. Those pieces appear to predate the September House vote, so I treated them as outdated. The bill was also folded into other legislation. The House Energy and Commerce Committee added it to H.R. 7389, the Motor Vehicle Modernization Act of 2026, which passed out of committee by a roll call vote of 48-1. It was also reported as part of the Build America 250 Act (H.R. 8870), the surface transportation reauthorization. Current highway authorities expire September 30, so that larger bill may become the vehicle for the AM provisions.

I could not confirm the current status of the surface transportation bill or whether the Senate has acted, so check Congress.gov for the latest.

The Eighth Circuit did vacate the FTC's click-to-cancel rule on July 8, 2025, days before enforcement was set to begin.

- **Holding and date:** On July 8, 2025, the US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit issued a per curiam opinion in Custom Communications, Inc. v. Federal Trade Commission. The court vacated the Rule in its entirety, which the FTC was poised to start enforcing in full on July 14, 2025.
- **Grounds:** The court ruled on procedural grounds. The agency did not publish a preliminary regulatory analysis once it determined the rule would impose compliance costs exceeding $100 million. The FTC failed to conduct a required regulatory analysis under Section 22 of the FTC Act.
- **Effect on businesses:** Companies that would have been subject to the Rule are now relieved of its specific compliance requirements, but are still subject to laws targeting negative option programs. That includes the Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act (ROSCA) and state autorenewal laws, as well as Section 5 of the FTC Act and analogous state unfair and deceptive trade practices (UDAP) laws.
- **State laws:** California's updated automatic renewal law took effect on July 1, 2025.

Sources differ slightly on the court's reasoning in one respect. One firm describes the FTC's failure as tied to an administrative law judge's cost finding, saying the court found that the FTC was required to prepare and publish a preliminary regulatory analysis once an administrative law judge concluded that the Rule's expected economic impact exceeded $100 million annually. The core outcome is the same across all sources. I did not check whether the ruling was later appealed or whether the FTC has since revived the rule, so consider that a gap in this search.

I ran one search. It didn't return a Reuters article, so the sources below are trade and news outlets, and none of them is Reuters.

- **Approval date and regulator:** The MIIT announced the first batch on December 15, 2025. It described the two models as the country's first L3 conditional autonomous driving vehicles to receive market access approval.
- **Changan model:** The approved Changan vehicle is the Deepal SL03, which is listed as the SC7000AAARBEV. Its autonomy covers a single lane on highways and urban expressways in congestion, with a 50 km/h cap. Its use is restricted to specific Chongqing sections, including the inner ring expressway and the new inner ring expressway.
- **BAIC model:** BAIC's Arcfox unit received approval for the BJ7001A61NBEV, which is marketed as the Arcfox Alpha S. Its use is limited to designated Beijing expressways, including parts of the airport north line and the Daxing Airport Expressway. Its speed cap is 80 km/h.
- **Scope and next step:** The approvals allow pilot road operation in designated areas, not general public use. Observers describe this as China moving L3 autonomous driving from testing toward early-stage commercial deployment.
- **Oversight:** MIIT said the vehicles will be operated by separate entities in Beijing and Chongqing, and authorities will closely monitor operations and safety.

content.content:
**China's Regulation on Management of Automobile Data Security (Trial)**

- **Dates:** The CAC and four other ministries approved the Regulation, which was published on August 16, 2021. It "will come into effect on October 1, 2021."
- **Scope:** It covers personal information and "Important Data" processed in automotive design, production, sales, use, and maintenance within mainland China. Covered parties include automakers, parts and software suppliers, distributors, maintenance firms, and mobility providers such as ride-hailing platforms.
- **Core principles:**
  - **In-car processing:** Data stays in the vehicle unless sending it outside is strictly necessary.
  - **No collection by default:** Collection is off for each drive unless the driver chooses otherwise.
  - **Proportionate sensing:** Camera and radar coverage and resolution must match the accuracy a service requires.
  - **Desensitization:** Data should be anonymized or de-identified wherever possible.
- **Important Data and cross-border transfer:** Important Data must be stored in China. If it must go overseas, a security assessment organized by regulators is required, and transfers must stay within the approved purpose, scope, method, data type, and scale.
- **Cabin and facial data:** Video and images captured outside vehicles that contain facial or license plate information are classed as Important Data. Biometrics such as faces, fingerprints, voiceprints, and heart rhythm may be collected only for driving safety, and only where sufficiently necessary. Processing sensitive data, including in-vehicle audio, video, and biometrics, requires separate consent, and deletion requests must be fulfilled within ten working days.
- **Reporting:** Processors handling Important Data must report their data security status to provincial CAC offices before December 15 each year.

This is a summary of the source article, not legal advice.

# Regulatory & Compliance Radar

**Status:** Seed v1. Researched 2026-10-11 via web search (plan-v2 pillar P2). Proposed only; PM review needed. Machine-readable version: `data/seed/regulations.json` (35 items).

## Purpose and scope

BMW's brief puts regulatory and homologation requirements **out of scope as outputs**. So this radar never produces a spec like "comply with UN R…". We use regulation in three ways only:

- **Context:** what will change in the car for the customer, per market, 2025 to about 2032.
- **Trigger:** a rule can trigger a *customer-facing* requirement, for example "core functions are reachable without touchscreen menus".
- **Gate:** a compliance fit check per derivative × market (`pass` / `warn` / `fail`), for example "flush electric-only door handles fail in China from 2027".

Rating programmes (Euro NCAP, C-NCAP, IIHS) are not law. We include them because a top rating is a de-facto market requirement.

**Conventions.** IDs match the JSON (`REG-<jurisdiction>-nn`). Trust tiers follow `knowledge-base.md`: T1 = official regulator or rating body, T2 = reputable press or law-firm briefing, T3 = blog, wiki or supplier. All sources were opened on 2026-10-11 unless marked otherwise. Dates are "new types / all new registrations".

---

## EU (and UNECE rules applied in the EU)

| ID | Rule | Type · status | Key dates | What changes for the driver | Tier |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| REG-EU-01 | Euro NCAP 2026 HMI: physical controls | Rating · in force | Rated from 2026-01-01 | Indicators, hazards, horn, wipers, full beam and speed set must be a button, stalk or one-tap control. A touch menu with more than 2 steps never passes. | T1 |
| REG-EU-02 | Euro NCAP 2026: DMS, ADAS annoyance, speed-limit accuracy, doors, EV fire | Rating · in force | 2026-01-01 | Assistance is tested on real roads for smoothness. Top scores need eye and head tracking. | T1 |
| REG-EU-03 | GSR2 (EU) 2019/2144: ISA, drowsiness, EDR, lane keeping, AEB | Law · in force | 2022-07 / 2024-07-07 | Speed-limit warning in every car. Drivers can switch it off, but it comes back at each start. 46% of UK drivers turn it off. | T1 |
| REG-EU-04 | GSR2: Advanced Driver Distraction Warning | Law · in force | 2024-07 / 2026-07-07 | A camera warns when the driver looks away too long. | T1 |
| REG-UN-01 | UN R155 / R156 cybersecurity and software updates | Law · in force | 2022-07 / 2024-07 | Owners must be told what each update does. Old electronics can force model withdrawal (Porsche 718 in the EU). | T2 |
| REG-UN-02 | UN R171 DCAS 01 series | Law · in force | In force 2025-09-26 | The car can start lane changes itself on motorways. Hands-off phases are allowed with eyes on the road. | T1 |
| REG-UN-03 | UN R171 DCAS 02 series | Law · adopted (WP.29, June 2026) | Entry into force not confirmed (~2027) | System manoeuvres off-highway and while hands-off. Stricter driver-disengagement checks. Adds speed limit assistance. | T2 |
| REG-EU-05 | EU Data Act | Law · in force | 2025-09-12 / design duty 2026-09-12 | Owners can access their car data and send it to a third party. | T2 |
| REG-EU-06 | Euro 7: brake dust, battery durability | Law · in force | 2026-11-29 / 2027-11-29 | Legal minimum battery health: 80% at 5 yr/100,000 km, 72% at 8 yr/160,000 km. Battery health is readable. | T1/T2 |
| REG-EU-07 | Batteries Regulation: battery passport | Law · in force | 2027-02-18 | A QR code on the battery opens a passport with capacity and expected lifetime. | T2 |
| REG-EU-08 | AFIR: charging payment and prices | Law · in force | 2024-04-13 / retrofit 2027-01-01 | Pay at fast chargers by bank card, no app needed. Price per kWh is shown. | T2 |
| REG-EU-09 | CO2 fleet targets: 2035 cut 100% → 90% | Law · **proposed** (Dec 2025) | Target year 2035 | PHEV and ICE may stay on sale after 2035. Parliament and Council outcome not verified. | T2 |
| REG-EU-10 | MVBER: repair data access | Law · in force | Until 2028-05-31 | Independent garages get equal access to repair data. | T2 |
| REG-EU-11 | Digital Fairness Act (subscriptions) | Law · debated | Proposal pending | Paid features will likely need cancel-as-easily-as-you-subscribe. | T2 |

## US

| ID | Rule | Type · status | Key dates | What changes for the driver | Tier |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| REG-US-01 | FMVSS 127: AEB incl. pedestrian, at night | Law · adopted, in litigation | 2029-09-01 (DOT plans +2 years) | Auto braking to avoid crashes up to 62 mph. Pedestrian detection in the dark. | T2 |
| REG-US-02 | FMVSS 208: rear seat belt reminder | Law · adopted | Front 2026-09-01 / rear 2027-09-01 | The driver is told when rear passengers are not buckled. | T1 |
| REG-US-03 | End of EV tax credits (30D, 45W) | Law · in force | Ended 2025-09-30 | No $7,500 EV credit for buyers or leases. | T1 |
| REG-US-04 | Section 232 tariff: 15% on EU cars | Law · in force | From 2025-08-01 | EU-built cars cost more in the US (input for content and packaging only, not pricing). | T2 |
| REG-US-05 | BIS connected-vehicle rule (China/Russia) | Law · in force | Software MY2027 / hardware MY2030 | No Chinese connectivity or driving software in US cars. China infotainment partners cannot be reused in the US. | T1 |
| REG-US-06 | AM Radio for Every Vehicle Act | Law · **proposed** (House passed 2026-09-15) | If enacted: ~2029 | AM radio standard in all new cars, EVs included. | T2 |
| REG-US-07 | IIHS partial automation safeguards | Rating · in force | Since 2024-03 | Buyers see whether assistance checks the driver. BMW's system was rated *poor* in 2024. | T1 |
| REG-US-08 | Subscriptions: FTC click-to-cancel vacated; state laws apply | Law · state laws in force | CA law 2025-07-01 | Subscriptions must still be easy to cancel (state law). | T2 |

## China

| ID | Rule | Type · status | Key dates | What changes for the driver | Tier |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| REG-CN-01 | GB 48001-2026 door handles | Mandatory std · adopted | In force 2027-01-01. New approvals by 2028-01-01. All models by 2029-01-01 | Every side door needs a handle that opens mechanically, without power. Electric-only flush handles end. | T2 |
| REG-CN-02 | MIIT post-SU7 measures: ADAS naming, OTA, beta, remote functions | Guidance · in force | Since 2025-04-16 | No "autonomous" or "smart driving" claims. No public betas. No unsupervised remote parking or summon. | T2 |
| REG-CN-03 | GB 47955-2026 L2 driver assistance | Mandatory std · adopted | 2027-01-01 | Driver monitoring is mandatory. Hands-off warning after 5 s. Function locked 30 min after misuse. | T2 |
| REG-CN-04 | MIIT/SAMR OTA and recall notice | Law · in force | Since 2025-02-25 | The owner must confirm each update and be told what changes. | T2 |
| REG-CN-05 | GB 4094 revision: physical controls | Mandatory std · adopted (final publication not verified) | 2027-07-01 (+13 months new types; 19-month grace for approved models) | Real buttons for gear, hazards, wipers, windows, ADAS on/off. Screen-only gear shifting banned. | T2 |
| REG-CN-06 | Auto data security (2021) and cross-border guidance (2026) | Law · in force | 2021-10-01; guidance 2026-02-03 | Cabin camera and voice data need opt-in. Location and camera data stay in China. | T2 |
| REG-CN-07 | NEV purchase tax halved; PHEV needs ≥100 km EV range | Law · in force | 2026-01-01 to 2027-12-31 | EVs and PHEVs pay 5% tax (cap ¥15,000 relief). Short-range PHEVs lose this. | T2 |
| REG-CN-08 | GB 38031-2025 battery "no fire, no explosion" | Mandatory std · in force | 2026-07-01 | EV batteries must not burn or explode after thermal runaway. | T2 |
| REG-CN-09 | Default acceleration ≥5 s 0-100 (draft) | Mandatory std · **proposed** | Draft 2025-11 | Fast EVs may start in a calm mode. Full power needs Sport. | T2 |
| REG-CN-10 | C-NCAP 2027 protocol | Rating · adopted | Released 2026-04-20 | More complex ADAS scenarios and V2X alerts. Physical controls and DMS also tightened (snippet only). | T2 |
| REG-CN-11 | GB 44495/44496 cybersecurity and software update | Mandatory std · **unverified dates** | 2026-01 or 2026-07 (new types) | China's version of R155/R156. | T3 |

## Japan and Korea (RoW)

| ID | Rule | Type · status | Key dates | What changes for the driver | Tier |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| REG-JP-01 | MLIT driver distraction and drowsiness monitoring | Law · **proposed** | New models 2031 / existing 2033 | A camera warns distracted drivers (6 s at 20-50 km/h, 3.5 s above). Imports included. Japan also applies UN R171. | T2 |
| REG-KR-01 | EV battery maker disclosure and certification | Law · in force | Measures 2024-09; certification from 2024-10 / 2025-02 | Buyers see battery maker, capacity and materials. | T2 |

---

## Top 8 customer-facing implications for successor BMWs (2028-2031)

1. **Tactile core controls, worldwide.** Euro NCAP 2026 already scores this. China's GB 4094 revision makes it law from July 2027: hazards, indicators, horn, wipers, gear selector, windows and ADAS on/off need real controls. Successor requirement: *"Core driving functions work blind, with a physical control, in every market."* This conflicts with screen-only Neue-Klasse-style minimalism. [REG-EU-01, REG-CN-05; euroncap.com SD-203 v1.1; CarNewsChina 2026-02-16; paultan.org 2026-07-10]
2. **Door handles: mechanical release in China from 2027.** Fully flush, electric-only handles fail GB 48001-2026. Euro NCAP also checks that electric handles work after a crash. Requirement: *"Doors open by hand from outside and inside, even without power, with a premium mechanical feel."* Design one global solution to avoid a China-only variant. [REG-CN-01, REG-EU-02; China Daily 2026-02-13; Euro NCAP 2025-11-26]
3. **Calm, accurate assistance, not nagging.** ISA and other GSR2 warnings annoy drivers: 46% of UK drivers switch ISA off. Euro NCAP now tests ADAS annoyance and speed-limit accuracy on real roads. Requirement: *"Speed-limit and attention warnings are accurate, quiet and easy to personalise in one press."* [REG-EU-03, REG-EU-02; Repairer Driven News / Which? 2025-03-27]
4. **Driver-monitoring camera everywhere.** It is required by EU ADDW (all new cars from July 2026) and China GB 47955 (2027), planned in Japan (2031), and needed for good Euro NCAP and IIHS scores (BMW was rated *poor* by IIHS in 2024). Requirement: *"Driver monitoring that is reliable, privacy-transparent and also used for comfort features."* [REG-EU-04, REG-CN-03, REG-JP-01, REG-US-07]
5. **Hands-off motorway (and later wider) assistance is now legal in the EU.** UN R171 01 series is in force since 2025-09-26. The 02 series, adopted June 2026, extends it beyond highways. In China the same features must be called *assisted driving*, with no public betas and no unsupervised remote parking. Requirement: *"Long-distance hands-off assistance with honest naming per market."* [REG-UN-02, REG-UN-03, REG-CN-02; UN depositary notification C.N.539.2025]
6. **Transparent software life.** UN R156 and China's OTA notice require owners to be told about and (in China) to confirm updates. Driving-related updates need approval in China. Requirement: *"Fewer, well-explained updates with plain-language notes and a stated update lifetime."* [REG-UN-01, REG-CN-04; CMS 2025-03-17]
7. **Battery health you can see and trust.** Euro 7 sets minimum battery durability. The EU battery passport arrives in Feb 2027. China requires "no fire, no explosion" batteries. Korea requires battery-maker disclosure. Requirement: *"State of health is shown in car and app, with a battery health promise and open battery facts."* [REG-EU-06, REG-EU-07, REG-CN-08, REG-KR-01]
8. **Market-split digital stack and data.** US law bans Chinese connectivity and ADS software from MY2027. China keeps important car data (location, camera) inside China and needs opt-in for cabin data. The EU Data Act gives owners their data. Requirement: *"Same BMW digital experience, with market-specific partners and clouds and a visible 'my data' control."* [REG-US-05, REG-CN-06, REG-EU-05]

Also relevant for powertrain and variant offers, but not top 8: China PHEVs need ≥100 km electric range for the tax break (REG-CN-07). US EV credits are gone (REG-US-03). The EU 2035 target may soften to 90% (REG-EU-09, proposed).

---

## Unverified / conflicting

- **Euro NCAP and eCall.** Press reports (S&P, others) list eCall among the 2026 physical-control functions. The official SD-203 v1.1 procedure lists indicator, hazard, horn, front/rear wiper, full beam and speed-assist set. We found no eCall entry. We follow the official text.
- **China door-handle dates.** One source says new models must comply "most requirements from 2027", another says new approvals by 2028-01-01. Both agree on 2029-01-01 for all models. Standard number GB 48001-2026 comes from search snippets (Gasgoo page returned 403).
- **China GB 4094 physical controls.** Reported dates are 2026-07, 2027-01 and 2027-07. The 2027-07-01 date has the most support. A "finalised draft" was reported in July 2026, but formal publication is not verified. The standard number is a revision of GB 4094-2016.
- **China L2 marketing terms.** The replacement wording is reported both as "L2 assisted driving" and as "combined assisted driving". The April 2025 rules come from a Reuters-reviewed meeting transcript, not a published legal text. Whether GB 47955 itself regulates naming is unclear.
- **GB 44495/44496 (China cybersecurity and OTA).** Dates conflict (2026-01 vs 2026-07 for new types; 2028 for existing). We did not open an official source (status `unverified`).
- **UN R171 02 series.** WP.29 adoption in June 2026 is confirmed by GlobalAutoRegs. The entry-into-force date is not. Norway objected that hands-off extensions bring DCAS close to automated driving.
- **Euro 7 battery thresholds.** The 80/72% figures come from press (EV inFocus 2024-03-14). The official dates come from the EP Legislative Observatory. EUR-Lex could not be fetched (blocked).
- **EU CO2 2035.** The 90% target is a Commission *proposal* (Dec 2025). The Parliament and Council positions in 2026 were not verified.
- **US FMVSS 127.** The 2029 deadline stands legally. DOT said (2026-03-23) it is preparing a rule giving two more years.
- **US BIS connected-vehicle rule.** No 2026 change was found. A Taylor Wessing (July 2026) item mentions a "tightening", but the page returned 403 and was not verified.
- **NEV purchase tax after 2027.** No extension was found. The Jiemian source page is undated.
- **C-NCAP 2027 physical-control and DMS items.** These come from a c-ncap.org.cn search snippet only. The opened Global NCAP article mentions only ADAS scenarios and C-V2X.
- **Korea battery certification.** It was planned for Feb 2025, with a pilot from Oct 2024. Current enforcement was not re-checked.
- **Not included (insufficient evidence found):**
  - illuminated grille or logo rules (UN R48/R149 work in GRE; no adopted text found);
  - camera-mirror changes;
  - AVAS changes;
  - accessibility rules specific to cars;
  - ISOFIX/i-Size changes affecting vehicles.

Rating programmes (Euro NCAP, C-NCAP, IIHS) are not law. We include them because a top rating is a de-facto market requirement.

**Conventions.** IDs match the JSON (`REG-<jurisdiction>-nn`). Trust tiers follow `knowledge-base.md`: T1 = official regulator or rating body, T2 = reputable press or law-firm briefing, T3 = blog, wiki or supplier. I wrote both files, with 35 regulations in total. The JSON is valid and every entry cites at least one source I opened on 2026-10-11, with a short quote. Items I could not fully confirm are marked as such, not presented as fact.

One thing to know first: `data/` is git-ignored, so `regulations.json` will not be committed as things stand. I did not edit code, the DB, any existing file or the confidential folder. The other uncommitted changes in the worktree come from other sessions.

**Counts per jurisdiction:**

| Jurisdiction | Items | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| EU | 11 | includes Euro NCAP |
| China | 11 | includes C-NCAP |
| US | 8 | includes IIHS |
| UNECE | 3 | R155/R156 combined, R171 01 series, R171 02 series |
| Japan | 1 | |
| Korea | 1 | |

By status: 22 in force, 7 adopted, 4 proposed, 1 debated, 1 unverified (China's cybersecurity and software-update standards GB 44495/44496, whose dates conflict). Trust tiers: the official items are T1 (Euro NCAP protocol, EU Commission, UN treaty notice, IRS, BIS, Federal Register, IIHS). Most China items are T2, from trade press and law firms.

**Top 8 implications for successor BMWs:**
1. **Physical core controls in every market.** Euro NCAP 2026 never accepts a touch menu deeper than 2 steps. China's revised GB 4094 requires real controls from July 2027, including the gear selector, windows and ADAS on/off; screen-only gear shifting is banned.
2. **Door handles that open mechanically.** China's GB 48001-2026 (in force 2027-01-01, all models by 2029-01-01) bans electric-only flush handles. Euro NCAP also checks that electric handles still work after a crash.
3. **Calm, accurate assistance.** EU speed-limit warnings annoy drivers (46% of UK drivers switch them off). Euro NCAP now tests real-road annoyance and speed-limit accuracy.
4. **A driver-monitoring camera everywhere.** Required in all new EU cars from July 2026, by China's L2 standard GB 47955-2026 from 2027, and planned in Japan for 2031/2033. IIHS rated BMW's current system "poor" in 2024.
5. **Hands-off motorway assistance is now legal in the EU.** UN R171 01 series has been in force since 2025-09-26. The 02 series, adopted June 2026, extends it beyond highways. In China it must be called "assisted driving", with no public betas and no unsupervised remote parking.
6. **Fewer, clearly explained software updates.** UN R156 requires telling owners what an update does. China requires owner confirmation of each update, and driving-related updates need government approval.
7. **Visible battery health and open battery facts.** Euro 7 sets a battery durability floor (80% at 5 years, 72% at 8 years). The EU battery passport arrives Feb 2027. China requires "no fire, no explosion" batteries from July 2026. Korea requires disclosure of the battery maker.
8. **A digital stack split by market.** The US bans Chinese connectivity and driving software from MY2027. China keeps important car data in-country and needs opt-in for cabin camera and voice data. The EU Data Act gives owners access to their car data.

**Surprising findings:**
- **Euro NCAP and eCall.** Press reports list eCall among the 2026 physical-control functions, but the official test procedure (SD-203 v1.1) does not include it. It does include full beam and cruise speed setting.
- **China's physical-control rule reaches into the cockpit.** The GB 4094 revision would put real controls on ADAS on/off and power windows, beyond what Euro NCAP asks. That directly conflicts with screen-only minimalism.
- **China's draft acceleration rule.** It would make cars start in a calm default mode (0–100 km/h no faster than 5 seconds). The ministry clarified it is not a performance cap. Still, it matters for i5 M60 / i7 M70-type variants.
- **China PHEVs now need at least 100 km of electric range** to keep the purchase-tax break in 2026–27.
- **US AM radio bill.** The House passed it on 2026-09-15, which could make AM radio standard equipment in new cars from about 2029.
- **US emergency braking deadline may slip.** The 2029 deadline still stands legally, but the DOT said in March 2026 that it is preparing a two-year delay.

The radar doc lists every open conflict in its "Unverified / conflicting" section. The main ones:
- China door-handle dates for new models: 2027 vs 2028.
- China physical-control effective date and final publication.
- China's replacement wording for "autonomous" in ads.
- No entry-into-force date yet for R171 02 series.
- Whether the EU Parliament and Council have adopted the 2035 CO2 change (still a proposal as far as I could verify).

Illuminated grilles, camera mirrors, pedestrian warning sound (AVAS), accessibility and child-seat (ISOFIX/i-Size) rules were left out because I found no adopted rules that change the car.

I wrote both files, with 35 regulations in total. The JSON is valid and every entry cites at least one source I opened on 2026-10-11, with a short quote. Items I could not fully confirm are marked as such, not presented as fact.

One thing to know first: `data/` is git-ignored, so `regulations.json` will not be committed as things stand. I did not edit code, the DB, any existing file or the confidential folder. The other uncommitted changes in the worktree come from other sessions.

By status: 22 in force, 7 adopted, 4 proposed, 1 debated, 1 unverified (China's cybersecurity and software-update standards GB 44495/44496, whose dates conflict). Trust tiers: the official items are T1 (Euro NCAP protocol, EU Commission, UN treaty notice, IRS, BIS, Federal Register, IIHS). Most China items are T2, from trade press and law firms.

**Top 8 implications for successor BMWs:**
1. **Physical core controls in every market.** Euro NCAP 2026 never accepts a touch menu deeper than 2 steps. China's revised GB 4094 requires real controls from July 2027, including the gear selector, windows and ADAS on/off; screen-only gear shifting is banned.
2. **Door handles that open mechanically.** China's GB 48001-2026 (in force 2027-01-01, all models by 2029-01-01) bans electric-only flush handles. Euro NCAP also checks that electric handles still work after a crash.
3. **Calm, accurate assistance.** EU speed-limit warnings annoy drivers (46% of UK drivers switch them off). Euro NCAP now tests real-road annoyance and speed-limit accuracy.
4. **A driver-monitoring camera everywhere.** Required in all new EU cars from July 2026, by China's L2 standard GB 47955-2026 from 2027, and planned in Japan for 2031/2033. IIHS rated BMW's current system "poor" in 2024.
5. **Hands-off motorway assistance is now legal in the EU.** UN R171 01 series has been in force since 2025-09-26. The 02 series, adopted June 2026, extends it beyond highways. In China it must be called "assisted driving", with no public betas and no unsupervised remote parking.
6. **Fewer, clearly explained software updates.** UN R156 requires telling owners what an update does. China requires owner confirmation of each update, and driving-related updates need government approval.
7. **Visible battery health and open battery facts.** Euro 7 sets a battery durability floor (80% at 5 years, 72% at 8 years). The EU battery passport arrives Feb 2027. China requires "no fire, no explosion" batteries from July 2026. Korea requires disclosure of the battery maker.
8. **A digital stack split by market.** The US bans Chinese connectivity and driving software from MY2027. China keeps important car data in-country and needs opt-in for cabin camera and voice data. The EU Data Act gives owners access to their car data.

**Surprising findings:**
- **Euro NCAP and eCall.** Press reports list eCall among the 2026 physical-control functions, but the official test procedure (SD-203 v1.1) does not include it. It does include full beam and cruise speed setting.
- **China's physical-control rule reaches into the cockpit.** The GB 4094 revision would put real controls on ADAS on/off and power windows, beyond what Euro NCAP asks. That directly conflicts with screen-only minimalism.
- **China's draft acceleration rule.** It would make cars start in a calm default mode (0–100 km/h no faster than 5 seconds). The ministry clarified it is not a performance cap. Still, it matters for i5 M60 / i7 M70-type variants.
- **China PHEVs now need at least 100 km of electric range** to keep the purchase-tax break in 2026–27.
- **US AM radio bill.** The House passed it on 2026-09-15, which could make AM radio standard equipment in new cars from about 2029.
- **US emergency braking deadline may slip.** The 2029 deadline still stands legally, but the DOT said in March 2026 that it is preparing a two-year delay.

The radar doc lists every open conflict in its "Unverified / conflicting" section. The main ones:
- China door-handle dates for new models: 2027 vs 2028.
- China physical-control effective date and final publication.
- China's replacement wording for "autonomous" in ads.
- No entry-into-force date yet for R171 02 series.
- Whether the EU Parliament and Council have adopted the 2035 CO2 change (still a proposal as far as I could verify).

Illuminated grilles, camera mirrors, pedestrian warning sound (AVAS), accessibility and child-seat (ISOFIX/i-Size) rules were left out because I found no adopted rules that change the car.
